questions.stimulus: Marine biologist Adriana Vergés and her colleagues have documented how warming ocean temperatures allow tropical herbivorous fish to expand their ranges into temperate kelp forests. Unlike native temperate species, these tropical browsers consume kelp blades at rates that exceed the algae's seasonal regrowth capacity, gradually transforming dense canopy habitats into sparse rocky reefs.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Range expansion by tropical herbivorous fish into warming temperate waters can deplete kelp forests faster than the kelp can regenerate.
Ocean warming affects rocky reefs more severely than it affects shallow coastal waters.
Temperate kelp forests grow more rapidly during warm seasons than tropical coral reefs do.
Native temperate fish species have adapted their diets to compete with arriving tropical browsers.

questions.explanation: Choice A accurately captures the central claim: warming temperatures enable tropical herbivorous fish to move into temperate kelp habitats, where their grazing outpaces kelp regrowth and converts dense canopies into sparse reefs. Choices C and D, and D introduce claims unsupported by the passage.

distractor_rationales.C: The text never compares the growth rate of temperate kelp forests with that of tropical coral reefs.
distractor_rationales.D: The text contrasts native temperate species with tropical browsers rather than stating native fish changed their diets.
distractor_rationales.B: Rocky reefs are described as the result of kelp loss, not as a pre-existing habitat more severely warmed.

questions.stimulus: In medieval European scriptoria, parchment made from calfskin (vellum) was prized for illuminated manuscripts because its smooth, low-lipid surface accepted gold leaf and mineral pigments evenly. However, archival multispectral imaging of twelfth-century parish registries—documents intended for routine administrative tracking rather than liturgical display—shows that scribes overwhelmingly selected coarser sheepskin parchment, which split easily if scraped to remove ink.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Because parish registries did not require decorative illumination, scribes prioritized sheepskin's resistance to undetected erasure and lower cost over vellum's smooth finish.
Multispectral imaging cannot distinguish between calfskin and sheepskin in illuminated liturgical manuscripts.
Twelfth-century scribes lacked access to mineral pigments when compiling administrative parish registries.
Vellum manuscripts deteriorated more rapidly in parish archives than sheepskin registries did.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts vellum (prized for decorative illumination) with sheepskin (used for administrative registries and prone to splitting if someone tried to scrape off ink). Thus, for administrative records where preventing tampering mattered more than gold leaf, sheepskin was advantageous.

distractor_rationales.C: The passage notes registries were not intended for liturgical display, not that pigments were unavailable.
distractor_rationales.D: Durability over centuries is not compared in the passage.
distractor_rationales.B: Multispectral imaging was successfully used to identify the parchment type.

questions.stimulus: Agronomists tested four cover-crop mixtures across 120 days to evaluate soil nitrogen retention and late-season weed suppression in upper Midwest plots. The researchers concluded that pairing a legume with a cereal grass allows farmers to capture nearly the full weed-suppression benefit of the grass without sacrificing the high nitrogen retention of the legume.
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.text: The Clover + Winter Rye mix achieved 86% weed suppression (close to Winter Rye's 89%) while retaining 64 kg/ha of nitrogen (close to Crimson Clover's 68 kg/ha).
Tillage Radish retained 51 kg/ha of nitrogen and suppressed 72% of weeds, outperforming Winter Rye in nitrogen retention.
Crimson Clover retained 68 kg/ha of nitrogen, the highest amount of any treatment in the 120-day trial.
Winter Rye alone suppressed 89% of weeds, whereas Crimson Clover alone suppressed only 54% of weeds.

questions.explanation: To support the claim that the pairing captures nearly the full weed-suppression benefit of the cereal grass without sacrificing the legume's nitrogen retention, Choice A directly cites the 50/50 mix's metrics (86% and 64 kg/ha) alongside the single-crop benchmarks (89% and 68 kg/ha).

distractor_rationales.D: Mentions only the single-crop extremes without citing the paired mixture.
distractor_rationales.B: Focuses on Tillage Radish, which is neither the legume nor the cereal grass in the conclusion.
distractor_rationales.C: Cites only Crimson Clover's nitrogen retention.

questions.stimulus: Literary critic Priya Nair argues that in nineteenth-century industrial novels, depictions of railway schedules do not merely provide realistic background detail; rather, they dramatize how standardized mechanical time reshaped characters' intimate perception of memory and obligation.
questions.prompt: Which quotation from a nineteenth-century novel would most directly illustrate Nair's claim?

choices.text: "Passengers waiting on the windy platform consulted the printed timetable nailed beside the ticket window before stowing their trunks."
"The new viaduct spanned forty arches of dressed limestone, carrying the morning express high above the canal barges that had served the valley for a century."
"Because the locomotive required fresh water every thirty miles, the company constructed iron tanks at each market town along the route."

"Even in the quiet parlor of his childhood home, Julian found himself measuring his father's pauses by the six-minute intervals of the junction bell, as though affection itself were a connection to be missed."

questions.explanation: Choice D directly shows railway scheduling ('six-minute intervals of the junction bell') reshaping a character's intimate emotional and familial perception ('measuring his father's pauses... as though affection itself were a connection to be missed').

distractor_rationales.B: Describes physical infrastructure and engineering rather than internal perception.
distractor_rationales.A: Provides literal background detail of passengers checking a timetable.
distractor_rationales.C: Describes mechanical logistics of steam locomotives.

questions.stimulus: Unlike traditional concrete, which releases carbon dioxide during limestone calcination, mycelium-based acoustic panels are grown by binding agricultural agricultural byproducts—such as hemp hurds or oat hulls—with the root-like fungal network of Ganoderma lucidum. Once heat-cured, the panels are fire-retardant, biodegradable, and absorb midrange office noise more effectively than fiberglass tiles.
questions.prompt: According to the text, how are mycelium-based acoustic panels produced?

choices.text: By heating limestone with fiberglass tiles to reduce midrange office noise.
By extracting carbon dioxide from traditional concrete during calcination.
By compressing synthetic polymers around live hemp plants.
By using fungal networks to bind agricultural plant byproducts and then heat-curing the material.

questions.source_name: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form)
questions.attribution: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form) (CC-BY-4.0)
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that the panels are grown by binding agricultural byproducts with the root-like fungal network and then heat-cured.

distractor_rationales.A: Limestone calcination and fiberglass tiles are mentioned as contrasting traditional materials.
distractor_rationales.C: Synthetic polymers are never mentioned.
distractor_rationales.B: Calcination is mentioned as releasing CO2 in traditional concrete.

questions.stimulus: Paleoclimatologists reconstructing monsoon intensity from stalagmite oxygen-isotope ratios ($\delta^{18}\text{O}$) long assumed that lower $\delta^{18}\text{O}$ values in cave calcite strictly reflect higher local rainfall volume. Recently, however, atmospheric tracer models demonstrated that shifts in the geographic moisture source—from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal—can lower precipitation $\delta^{18}\text{O}$ by up to 3 per mil even when total local rainfall remains constant.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Oxygen-isotope ratios in cave calcite remain constant regardless of changes in regional monsoon circulation.
Stalagmites formed near the Arabian Sea grow more rapidly than those formed near the Bay of Bengal.
Atmospheric tracer models are less reliable than stalagmite calcite measurements for dating ancient cave formations.
Interpreting stalagmite $\delta^{18}\text{O}$ records as a direct measure of local rainfall volume may be inaccurate if concurrent changes in moisture-source pathways are not accounted for.

questions.explanation: Because changes in the geographic moisture source can alter $\delta^{18}\text{O}$ by up to 3 per mil without any change in local rainfall volume, attributing lower $\delta^{18}\text{O}$ solely to local rainfall volume can be misleading unless source-pathway changes are considered.

distractor_rationales.B: Stalagmite growth rate is not discussed.
distractor_rationales.A: Contradicts the text, which explains two different factors that change $\delta^{18}\text{O}$.
distractor_rationales.C: Radiometric dating of caves is not the subject of the passage.

questions.stimulus: Whereas early portable seismographs required delicate mechanical pendulums that could be disrupted by minor jostling during transport, modern solid-state accelerometers are remarkably _______, functioning reliably even when dropped from reconnaissance aircraft into volcanic craters.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: 'Resilient' means able to withstand shock or rough conditions, which contrasts directly with 'delicate' pendulums and matches 'functioning reliably even when dropped from reconnaissance aircraft'.

distractor_rationales.C: 'Ambiguous' means open to multiple interpretations.
distractor_rationales.D: 'Ephemeral' means short-lived.
distractor_rationales.A: 'Tentative' means hesitant or provisional.

questions.stimulus: Architect Lina Bo Bardi rejected the notion that museum display cases should isolate artworks from everyday life; instead, at the São Paulo Museum of Art, she mounted paintings on transparent tempered-glass easels so visitors could move freely among the works in a _______ spatial arrangement.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: 'Nonhierarchical' describes an arrangement without fixed rank or forced sequence, matching Bo Bardi's rejection of isolating walls and her support for visitors moving freely among transparent easels.

distractor_rationales.B: 'Clandestine' means secretive.
distractor_rationales.D: 'Redundant' means repetitive or unnecessary.
distractor_rationales.A: 'Perfunctory' means carried out with minimal effort.

questions.stimulus: Far from offering a _______ endorsement of algorithmic credit scoring, economist Safiya Patel demonstrates that while automated underwriting reduces processing delays for standard mortgages, it systematically amplifies historical data gaps for first-generation rural borrowers.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: 'Univocal' (or unqualified/unambiguous) fits the contrast: Patel does not give a single-sided endorsement, because she highlights both a benefit (faster processing) and a systemic flaw (amplifying data gaps).

distractor_rationales.A: 'Mendacious' means untruthful.
distractor_rationales.B: 'Parsimonious' means stingy or sparing.
distractor_rationales.C: 'Derivative' means unoriginal.

questions.stimulus: Many popular accounts of the 1925 serum run to Nome credit a single lead sled dog, Balto, with saving the isolated Alaskan town from a diphtheria outbreak. Historian Gay Salisbury and Laney Salisbury, however, emphasize that the 674-mile relay involved twenty mushers and roughly 150 dogs, with Leonhard Seppala's team—led by Togo—covering the longest and most hazardous crossing over Norton Sound.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It chronicles the chronological stages of a medical emergency and then proposes a policy to prevent future outbreaks.
It compares two competing scientific explanations for a phenomenon and argues that neither is complete.
It presents a widely held simplified view of a historical event and then offers historical details that complicate that view.
It praises an individual achievement and then explains why contemporary observers ignored it.

questions.explanation: The first sentence states a popular simplified narrative (crediting a single dog, Balto), and the second sentence introduces historians' broader evidence (20 mushers, 150 dogs, and Togo's longest hazardous leg) that complicates that simplified view.

distractor_rationales.A: No future public health policy is proposed.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage is historical, not a comparison of competing scientific theories.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage corrects a narrow popular focus rather than claiming the event was ignored.

questions.stimulus:
Text 1
Urban ecologist Marcus Vance contends that planting non-native drought-tolerant street trees in arid cities is an ecological mistake. Because native insect herbivores have not co-evolved with exotic foliage, non-native canopies support up to 70% fewer caterpillar species, depriving migratory songbirds of essential protein during spring stopovers.

Text 2
Landscape hydrologist Elena Rostova notes that in heavily paved metropolitan heat islands, soil compaction and radiant heat create microclimates several degrees hotter and drier than the surrounding native desert. In her multi-year survey of Phoenix boulevards, several native riparian tree species suffered high canopy dieback, whereas selected non-native Mediterranean oaks maintained dense shade that cooled adjacent sidewalks by 6°C and allowed understory native shrubs to survive.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would Rostova (Text 2) most likely respond to Vance's argument (Text 1)?

choices.text: By disputing Vance's finding that migratory songbirds rely on caterpillars during spring stopovers.
By arguing that urban planners should replace all street trees with artificial shade structures to conserve water.
By agreeing that non-native Mediterranean oaks should be removed from arid cities immediately.

By pointing out that in extreme urban microclimates where native trees struggle to survive, resilient non-native trees can provide microclimate cooling that indirectly supports native understory plants.

questions.source_name: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form)
questions.attribution: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form) (CC-BY-4.0)
questions.explanation: Rostova shows that paved urban heat islands are harsher than surrounding deserts, causing some native trees to die back while hardy non-native trees provide shade that cools sidewalks and helps native understory shrubs survive.

distractor_rationales.A: Rostova does not address or dispute songbird diet.
distractor_rationales.B: Artificial shade structures are never mentioned.
distractor_rationales.C: Rostova highlights the benefits of Mediterranean oaks in Phoenix boulevards.

questions.stimulus: In 1899, physicist Hertha Ayrton read her paper on the behavior of electric arcs before the Institution of Electrical Engineers in _______ she became the first woman invited to become a full member of the prestigious society.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The text contains two independent clauses: 'In 1899, physicist Hertha Ayrton read her paper... in London' and 'shortly thereafter, she became the first woman...'. A semicolon properly joins the two independent clauses, followed by a comma after the introductory transition phrase 'shortly thereafter'.

distractor_rationales.C: Creates a comma splice between two independent clauses.
distractor_rationales.D: Creates a fused (run-on) sentence with no punctuation between independent clauses.
distractor_rationales.A: Creates a comma splice.

questions.stimulus: The acoustics of ancient Greek amphitheaters—most notably Epidaurus, whose limestone seating tiers filter out low-frequency background wind noise while amplifying high-frequency vocal consonants—_______ modern architectural engineers for decades.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'The acoustics' requires a plural verb, and the temporal phrase 'for decades' calls for the present perfect tense ('have intrigued'). Choices C and D, and D are all singular verbs.

distractor_rationales.C: Singular verb 'has' does not agree with plural subject 'acoustics'.
distractor_rationales.D: Singular verb 'is' does not agree with 'acoustics' or fit 'for decades'.
distractor_rationales.B: Singular verb 'intrigues' does not agree with 'acoustics'.

questions.stimulus: Calibrated using laser interferometry in an underground vacuum chamber, _______ can detect gravitational-wave strain amplitudes smaller than one ten-thousandth the diameter of a proton.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: gravitational-wave strain amplitudes at the LIGO observatory
physicists' measurements of the LIGO observatory's silica mirrors
it is the LIGO observatory's suspended silica mirrors that
the suspended silica mirrors of the LIGO observatory

questions.explanation: The introductory participial phrase 'Calibrated using laser interferometry in an underground vacuum chamber' must modify the noun immediately following the comma. 'The suspended silica mirrors of the LIGO observatory' are what are calibrated and can detect the strain amplitudes.

distractor_rationales.A: Creates a dangling modifier: strain amplitudes are not calibrated in a vacuum chamber.
distractor_rationales.B: Measurements are not physical objects calibrated in an underground vacuum chamber that themselves detect strain.
distractor_rationales.C: Expletive 'it' cannot be modified by 'Calibrated using laser interferometry'.

questions.stimulus: Botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer observes that when sweetgrass (Hierochloe odorata) is harvested selectively by _______ the plant responds with vigorous compensatory tillering, producing denser shoots the following spring than unharvested plots do.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.source_name: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form)
questions.attribution: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form) (CC-BY-4.0)
questions.explanation: Within the 'that' clause, 'when sweetgrass (Hierochloe odorata) is harvested selectively by hand' is a dependent adverbial clause preceding the main clause 'the plant responds...'. A comma is required after 'hand' to separate the dependent clause from the independent clause.

distractor_rationales.B: A semicolon cannot separate a dependent 'when' clause from its main clause.
distractor_rationales.A: Omits the necessary comma after an introductory dependent clause.
distractor_rationales.D: An em dash is inappropriate when no paired dash or abrupt break exists.

questions.stimulus: Early twentieth-century glacialogists assumed that subglacial lakes beneath the Antarctic ice sheet were hydrologically isolated basins that remained stagnant for millions of years. _______ satellite laser altimetry in the 2000s revealed rapid rises and falls in the ice surface above Lake Whillans, proving that subglacial water periodically flushes through interconnected channels.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The second sentence overturns the assumption described in the first sentence ('hydrologically isolated... stagnant' vs. 'periodically flushes through interconnected channels'). 'However,' signals this contrast.

distractor_rationales.C: 'Consequently,' indicates cause and effect.
distractor_rationales.B: 'Similarly,' indicates comparison of alike ideas.
distractor_rationales.D: 'For instance,' introduces an example of the preceding claim rather than a refutation.

questions.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Sodium-ion batteries use abundant sodium salts rather than lithium and cobalt.
- Current commercial sodium-ion cells have a gravimetric energy density of 140–160 Wh/kg, compared with 240–280 Wh/kg for nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) lithium-ion cells.
- Sodium-ion cells retain over 88% of their discharge capacity at -20°C, whereas standard lithium-ion cells often drop below 65% capacity at that temperature.
- Because stationary grid storage facilities do not move, battery weight is far less important than cold-weather reliability and raw-material cost.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain why sodium-ion batteries are particularly well suited for stationary cold-climate grid storage despite having lower energy density than NMC lithium-ion cells. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: At -20°C, standard lithium-ion cells often drop below 65% discharge capacity, while sodium-ion batteries have an energy density of 140–160 Wh/kg.
NMC lithium-ion cells achieve an energy density of 240–280 Wh/kg, whereas sodium-ion cells use abundant sodium salts instead of lithium and cobalt.

Although sodium-ion batteries have a lower energy density (140–160 Wh/kg) than NMC lithium-ion cells, their heavier weight matters little in stationary grid facilities, where their low-cost sodium materials and >88% capacity retention at -20°C are major advantages.
Stationary grid storage facilities do not move, so engineers must choose between NMC lithium-ion batteries and sodium-ion batteries.

questions.explanation: Choice C synthesizes all parts of the prompt: acknowledging the lower energy density, explaining why weight is unimportant for stationary storage, and highlighting both cold-weather retention (>88% at -20°C) and abundant sodium materials.

distractor_rationales.B: Omits cold-weather performance and stationary grid storage altogether.
distractor_rationales.A: Juxtaposes statistics without explaining why stationary grid storage favors sodium-ion.
distractor_rationales.D: Fails to mention energy density, cold-weather performance, or material cost.

questions.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1977, the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft launched carrying the Golden Record, a 12-inch gold-plated copper phonograph disc.
- The committee led by Carl Sagan selected 115 analog-encoded images and 90 minutes of audio.
- Acoustic engineer Timothy Ferris oversaw the mastering of the record at 16 2/3 revolutions per minute (rpm) rather than the standard 33 1/3 rpm LP speed.
- Halving the rotational speed doubled the playing time that could fit into the disc's physical grooves, though it slightly reduced high-frequency audio fidelity.
questions.prompt: The student wants to emphasize the engineering trade-off involved in mastering the Voyager Golden Record. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Timothy Ferris oversaw the mastering of the Golden Record, which spun at 16 2/3 revolutions per minute rather than the standard 33 1/3 rpm.
Carl Sagan's committee included both analog-encoded images and audio recordings on the 12-inch copper phonograph disc.

By mastering the Voyager Golden Record at 16 2/3 rpm instead of 33 1/3 rpm, Timothy Ferris doubled the audio duration that could fit on the disc at the cost of a slight reduction in high-frequency fidelity.
Launched in 1977 aboard Voyager 1 and 2, the 12-inch gold-plated copper Golden Record contained 115 images and 90 minutes of audio selected by Carl Sagan's committee.

questions.source_name: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form)
questions.attribution: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form) (CC-BY-4.0)
questions.explanation: Choice C explicitly states the engineering trade-off: halving the speed from 33 1/3 rpm to 16 2/3 rpm doubled the audio capacity while sacrificing some high-frequency fidelity.

distractor_rationales.D: Provides general background without mentioning the engineering trade-off.
distractor_rationales.A: States the speed difference without explaining the benefit or cost.
distractor_rationales.B: Describes the contents without mentioning any trade-off.

questions.stimulus: A botanical conservatory maintains a tropical orchid room by running a misting system. The reservoir starts the day with $480$ liters of distilled water and releases $15$ liters per hour. If $W$ represents the volume of water remaining after $t$ hours, and $W = 480 - 15t$, after how many hours will exactly $195$ liters remain?
questions.prompt: What is the value of $t$ when $W = 195$?
questions.explanation: Substitute $W = 195$ into the linear equation: $195 = 480 - 15t$. Subtract $195$ from $480$: $15t = 285$. Divide both sides by $15$: $t = 285 / 15 = 19$ hours.

distractor_rationales.C: Result of arithmetic error $255 / 15 = 17$.
distractor_rationales.D: Result of $315 / 15 = 21$.
distractor_rationales.A: Total time to empty the entire $480$-liter tank ($480 / 15 = 32$).

questions.skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
questions.prompt: If $(x, y)$ is the solution to the given system of equations, what is the value of $x + y$?
questions.explanation: Multiply the second equation by $2$ to eliminate $y$: $10x - 4y = 34$. Adding this to the first equation gives $13x = 65$, so $x = 5$. Substituting $x = 5$ into $3x + 4y = 31$ gives $15 + 4y = 31$, so $y = 4$. Therefore $x + y = 5 + 4 = 9$.

questions.stimulus: A municipal bike-share program charges a monthly membership fee plus a constant usage rate per minute for rides exceeding $30$ minutes. The function $C(m) = 18 + 0.15m$ gives the total monthly cost $C(m)$, in dollars, for a member who accumulates $m$ overage minutes during the month.
questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation of the number $18$ in this context?

choices.text: The total cost, in dollars, of an $18$-minute bike ride.
The charge, in dollars, for each additional minute beyond $30$ minutes.
The fixed monthly membership fee, in dollars, when a member has $0$ overage minutes.
The maximum number of overage minutes included in the base plan.

questions.explanation: In the linear model $C(m) = 18 + 0.15m$, the constant term $18$ is the $y$-intercept $C(0)$, representing the fixed monthly membership fee before any overage minutes are incurred.

distractor_rationales.B: The per-minute overage rate is $0.15$, the slope of the linear function.
distractor_rationales.D: The variable $m$ counts overage minutes; $18$ is measured in dollars.
distractor_rationales.A: The function models monthly cost for $m$ overage minutes, not the cost of an $18$-minute trip.

questions.skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
questions.stimulus: A bakery produces loaves of sourdough bread that each require $0.6$ kilograms of flour and batches of brioche rolls that each require $0.4$ kilograms of flour. The bakery has at most $36$ kilograms of flour available for the morning bake and must prepare at least $30$ loaves of sourdough bread to fulfill standing restaurant orders.
questions.prompt: If $s$ represents the number of sourdough loaves and $b$ represents the number of brioche batches, what is the maximum number of brioche batches the bakery can produce?
questions.explanation: The flour constraint is $0.6s + 0.4b \le 36$ with $s \ge 30$. To maximize $b$, use the minimum required sourdough loaves $s = 30$: $0.6(30) + 0.4b \le 36 \Rightarrow 18 + 0.4b \le 36 \Rightarrow 0.4b \le 18 \Rightarrow b \le 45$.

distractor_rationales.C: This is the minimum number of sourdough loaves required, not the maximum number of brioche batches.
distractor_rationales.D: Divides $36$ by $0.6$ instead of accounting for the sourdough requirement.
distractor_rationales.A: Assumes $s = 0$, ignoring the constraint $s \ge 30$.

questions.skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
questions.prompt: In the system of equations above, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
questions.source_name: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form)
questions.attribution: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form) (CC-BY-4.0)
questions.explanation: A system of two linear equations has infinitely many solutions when one equation is a non-zero constant multiple of the other. Comparing the $y$-coefficients and constant terms, $-18 = 3(-6)$ and $42 = 3(14)$. Therefore the second equation is $3$ times the first equation, so $15 = 3k$, which gives $k = 5$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is equivalent to the given expression?
questions.explanation: Distribute the subtraction sign across the second polynomial: $2x^2 - 5x + 3 - x^2 + 4x + 7$. Combine like terms: $(2x^2 - x^2) + (-5x + 4x) + (3 + 7) = x^2 - x + 10$.

distractor_rationales.A: Fails to distribute the negative sign to $-4x$ and $-7$.
distractor_rationales.B: Distributes the negative sign to $-4x$ but not to $-7$.
distractor_rationales.D: Adds the $x^2$ terms instead of subtracting.

questions.stimulus: The height $h(t)$, in meters above the ground, of a weather probe launched vertically from a platform is modeled by the function $h(t) = -5t^2 + 40t + 12$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after launch.
questions.prompt: What is the maximum height, in meters, reached by the probe?
questions.explanation: For a quadratic function $h(t) = at^2 + bt + c$ with $a < 0$, the maximum occurs at the vertex $t = -b/(2a) = -40 / (2 \cdot (-5)) = 4$ seconds. Evaluating $h(4) = -5(4)^2 + 40(4) + 12 = -80 + 160 + 12 = 92$ meters.

distractor_rationales.D: Omits the initial platform height of $12$ meters.
distractor_rationales.A: Evaluates $h(2)$ instead of the vertex $h(4)$.
distractor_rationales.C: Gives the time $t = 4$ seconds at which the maximum occurs rather than the maximum height.

questions.skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
questions.prompt: What is the positive difference between the two solutions to the given quadratic equation?
questions.explanation: Factor the quadratic expression: $(x - 3)(x - 8) = 0$. The solutions are $x = 8$ and $x = 3$. The positive difference between the two solutions is $8 - 3 = 5$.

questions.stimulus: A culture of bioluminescent bacteria initially contains $2{,}500$ cells. Under controlled nutrient conditions, the population doubles every $3$ hours.
questions.prompt: Which function $P(t)$ best models the number of bacteria in the culture $t$ hours after the start of the observation?
questions.explanation: Because the population doubles every $3$ hours, the growth factor per $3$-hour period is $2$, and the number of $3$-hour doubling periods in $t$ hours is $t/3$. Thus $P(t) = 2{,}500(2)^{t/3}$.

distractor_rationales.D: Models a population that doubles $3$ times per hour (every $20$ minutes).
distractor_rationales.A: Uses base $3$ (tripling) instead of base $2$ (doubling).
distractor_rationales.C: Adds the exponential term instead of multiplying the initial population.

questions.skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
questions.prompt: In the given equation, $c$ is a constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the value of $c$?
questions.source_name: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form)
questions.attribution: HDSAT Benchmark Simulation Set A (Released Practice Form) (CC-BY-4.0)
questions.explanation: A quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has exactly one real solution when its discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ equals $0$. Here $a = 2$ and $b = -12$, so $(-12)^2 - 4(2)(c) = 0 \Rightarrow 144 - 8c = 0 \Rightarrow c = 18$.

questions.skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.stimulus: The table shows the daily particulate matter readings (in micrograms per cubic meter) recorded at an air-quality station over $6$ days. On Day 7, a reading of $92$ micrograms per cubic meter is recorded due to a regional dust event.
questions.prompt: By how much does the mean of the $7$-day dataset exceed the median of the $7$-day dataset?
questions.explanation: The ordered $7$-day dataset is $14, 18, 21, 21, 25, 33, 92$. The median (fourth value) is $21$. The sum of all $7$ readings is $14 + 18 + 21 + 21 + 25 + 33 + 92 = 224$, so the mean is $224 / 7 = 32$. The mean exceeds the median by $32 - 21 = 11$.

questions.stimulus: A quality-control engineer inspected $240$ solar panels from two production lines and recorded the results in the table.
questions.prompt: If one of the panels that passed inspection is selected at random, what is the probability that it was manufactured on Line A?
questions.explanation: The condition restricts the sample space to the $225$ panels that passed inspection. Of those, $132$ came from Line A. The conditional probability is $132 / 225 = 44 / 75$ (dividing numerator and denominator by $3$).

distractor_rationales.D: Computes $132 / 140$, the probability that a Line A panel passed.
distractor_rationales.C: Computes $132 / 240$, the unconditional proportion of all panels that came from Line A and passed.
distractor_rationales.A: Computes $140 / 240$, the proportion of all panels produced on Line A.

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.stimulus: A transit authority surveyed a random sample of $400$ weekday commuter-rail riders in a metropolitan region. Based on the sample, the authority estimated that $64\%$ of all weekday commuter-rail riders in the region use mobile ticketing, with an associated margin of error of $4.5\%$ at the $95\%$ confidence level.
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion from the survey?

choices.text: It is plausible that the actual percentage of all weekday commuter-rail riders in the region who use mobile ticketing is between $59.5\%$ and $68.5\%$.
If the transit authority surveyed another $400$ riders, the new sample proportion would be guaranteed to equal $64\%$.
Among the $400$ sampled riders, between $59.5\%$ and $68.5\%$ stated that they were $95\%$ satisfied with mobile ticketing.
Exactly $64\%$ of all transit riders across every mode of transportation in the region use mobile ticketing.

questions.explanation: A sample estimate of $64\%$ with a margin of error of $\pm 4.5\%$ yields a plausible interval of $64\% - 4.5\% = 59.5\%$ to $64\% + 4.5\% = 68.5\%$ for the population from which the random sample was drawn (weekday commuter-rail riders in the region).

distractor_rationales.D: Overgeneralizes beyond commuter-rail riders and treats the sample estimate as an exact population value.
distractor_rationales.C: Confuses the confidence level and margin of error with individual rider satisfaction.
distractor_rationales.B: New random samples vary due to sampling variability; they are not guaranteed to match $64\%$.

questions.stimulus: A right circular cylinder has a base radius of $4$ centimeters and a height of $9$ centimeters. The volume of the cylinder can be written in the form $k\pi$ cubic centimeters, where $k$ is a constant.
questions.prompt: What is the value of $k$?
questions.explanation: The volume of a right circular cylinder is $V = \pi r^2 h$. Substituting $r = 4$ and $h = 9$ gives $V = \pi (4)^2 (9) = 144\pi$ cubic centimeters, so $k = 144$.

questions.stimulus: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle, the length of side $AC$ is $12$, and the length of hypotenuse $AB$ is $15$.
questions.prompt: What is the value of $\sin A$?
questions.explanation: By the Pythagorean theorem, $BC = \sqrt{15^2 - 12^2} = \sqrt{225 - 144} = \sqrt{81} = 9$. Side $BC$ is opposite angle $A$, so $\sin A = \text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse} = 9 / 15 = 3 / 5$.

distractor_rationales.A: Equals $\cos A = 12/15 = 4/5$.
distractor_rationales.B: Equals $\tan A = 9/12 = 3/4$.
distractor_rationales.D: Equals $\cot A = 12/9 = 4/3$, which is greater than $1$.

questions.prompt: The equation above represents a circle in the $xy$-plane. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: Complete the square for $x$ and $y$: $(x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 8y + 16) = 11 + 9 + 16 \Rightarrow (x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 36$. In standard form $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$, we have $r^2 = 36$, so the radius is $r = 6$.

distractor_rationales.B: Gives $r^2 = 36$ instead of $r = 6$.
distractor_rationales.A: Takes the square root of the constant term before completing the square.
distractor_rationales.D: Finds $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, omitting the $11$ on the right-hand side.

questions.explanation: The area of a sector with central angle $\theta$ radians is $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$. Substituting $r = 10$ and $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{5}$ gives $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}(100)\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right) = 20\pi$. Thus $m = 20$.

questions.stimulus:

Text 2: Soil chemist Nowsherwan Ali counters that on the clay-heavy fields he studies, standing residue keeps the surface so wet and cold each spring that nitrogen mineralization begins two weeks late, costing more yield than the added moisture is worth.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would Ali most likely respond to Ferro?

choices.text: He would point out that Ferro's farms are too small to matter statistically.
He would agree that standing residue raises winter moisture but argue that on wet clay soils that same moisture delays spring nitrogen release and lowers yields.

He would insist that residue be chopped and incorporated regardless of results.

questions.explanation: Ali accepts the moisture mechanism (that is Ferro's own point) and flips it: on his soils, the same moisture is a cost. Option D captures agreement-plus-reversal.

distractor_rationales.C: He does not deny moisture effects; he disagrees about their value on clay.
distractor_rationales.D: He never proposes chopping residue; he weighs trade-offs.
distractor_rationales.A: He critiques the agronomic trade-off, not study size.

questions.stimulus: Along the California coast, purple sea urchins have multiplied in recent decades, grazing kelp holdfasts until once-dense forests become bare rock. Biologists note that the urchin boom followed the loss of sea otters, which eat urchins, to disease and historic hunting. questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The presence of sea otters helps keep kelp forests from being overgrazed by urchins.
Transplanting sea otters restores kelp forests wherever they are attempted.
Sea urchins improve kelp growth by clearing competing algae from holdfasts.
Kelp forests are declining mainly because ocean temperatures have risen.

questions.explanation: The passage links the loss of otters to an urchin boom and then to kelp loss, and it says otter transplants work only under limited conditions.

distractor_rationales.C: The text presents urchins as grazers that strip kelp, not as helpers.
distractor_rationales.D: Temperature is never offered as the cause; the otter loss is.
distractor_rationales.B: The text limits success to sites where urchin numbers were already low.

questions.stimulus: Roman harbour concrete has survived two millennia of wave action that erodes modern port cement in decades. Analysis of cores shows the material contains lumps of lime that were never fully mixed. When cracks form, water dissolves calcium from these lumps and precipitates new minerals that seal the crack. questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Modern port cement fails because it contains too much calcium.
Lime lumps once dismissed as a mixing flaw are what allow Roman harbour concrete to heal itself.
Roman concrete was weaker than modern cement but lasted longer by accident.
Roman builders deliberately added cracks to their concrete to test it.

questions.explanation: The core claim is a reversal: the lime lumps were read as a defect and are now understood to supply the mineral that seals cracks.

distractor_rationales.C: The text does not compare initial strength, only durability.
distractor_rationales.A: Calcium in the Roman lumps is described as helpful, not as a fault in modern cement.
distractor_rationales.D: Cracks are described as something the material repairs, not something builders created.

questions.stimulus: A returning honeybee that has found a rich patch of flowers performs a looping dance on the comb. choices.text: Honeybees find flowers by following the scent of nectar through the hive.

Bees can dance accurately only when they can see the sun directly.
The length of the dance tells other bees how many flowers are available.

questions.explanation: The rotated-hive experiment is the decisive evidence: when gravity and sky disagree, the bees follow gravity, so direction is encoded against vertical.

distractor_rationales.A: Scent is not mentioned; the dance is the mechanism described.
distractor_rationales.D: Duration is said to encode distance, not abundance.
distractor_rationales.C: The experiment shows the dance works in darkness by using gravity.

questions.stimulus: Antarctic ice preserves air bubbles from the atmosphere of past millennia. By measuring the ratio of oxygen isotopes in the ice itself and the trapped carbon dioxide in the bubbles, researchers reconstruct temperature and greenhouse gas levels for the same moment. questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Climate models rely on ice cores because direct temperature measurements are unavailable today.
Ice cores provide a paired record of ancient temperature and carbon dioxide that supports climate modeling.
Air bubbles in ice contain only oxygen, not carbon dioxide.
Ice cores show that temperature and carbon dioxide levels are unrelated over long periods.

questions.explanation: One core yields both signals for the same moment, and the correlation across glacial cycles is what makes the record useful for models.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says the two records move together.
distractor_rationales.C: Carbon dioxide in the bubbles is the second measurement described.
distractor_rationales.A: The cores reconstruct the past; the text does not claim present measurements are missing.

distractor_rationales.A: Breeders use wild species precisely to widen resistance.

questions.stimulus: For thousands of years, people in many fire-prone regions set small fires in cool seasons. questions.stimulus: Lithium is extracted from brines pumped from beneath salt flats. The process evaporates water in shallow ponds over many months, leaving lithium salts behind. questions.stimulus: Iron gall ink, used for centuries on parchment, corrodes the paper from within as it ages: the iron and acid it contains attack cellulose. Conservators once treated affected pages with alkaline solutions, which slowed the decay but sometimes darkened the ink. questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Gel treatments remove the ink from the page to protect the parchment.

A targeted gel treatment neutralises corrosive ink without damaging the rest of the page.
Iron gall ink is harmless once it has dried on parchment.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a broad treatment that had a side effect with a precise one that confines the chemical to where it is needed.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the solutions did slow decay, but sometimes darkened the ink.
distractor_rationales.D: The text describes the ink attacking cellulose as it ages.
distractor_rationales.A: The gel delivers a neutralising agent to the ink lines; it does not remove them.

distractor_rationales.C: The text notes the calls carry differently at midday, when the air is turbulent.

questions.stimulus: Satellite measurements of surface temperature show that blocks with mature tree canopy can be several degrees cooler than treeless blocks nearby. distractor_rationales.C: The text says saplings produce little cooling for years.
distractor_rationales.D: Vapour is described as cooling the air, not warming it.

questions.stimulus: Norse sagas describe sailors finding the sun on cloudy days with a crystal. Some translucent minerals split light into two beams whose relative brightness changes with the angle to polarised skylight; a navigator could rotate such a stone until the beams matched to locate the sun's position. Experiments with calcite have reproduced the effect, though no such stone has been recovered from a Norse ship.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A polarising crystal could locate the sun in cloudy weather, though the evidence that Norse sailors used one is indirect.
Sagas are unreliable because they describe crystals that cannot exist.
Polarised skylight is visible only when the sky is completely clear.
Calcite has been found aboard several Norse ships, confirming how sailors navigated.

questions.explanation: The passage sets a saga claim beside a demonstrable optical effect, then notes the missing physical evidence, which keeps the conclusion provisional.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says no such stone has been recovered from a Norse ship.
distractor_rationales.B: The effect has been reproduced with calcite, so such crystals do exist.
distractor_rationales.C: The whole point is that the technique works under cloud, when direct sunlight is hidden.

questions.stimulus: Most antibiotics in use today were first found in soil microorganisms that produce them to compete with neighbors. That same soil is now a reservoir of resistance genes, many of them ancient and unrelated to clinical drug use. When resistance genes from soil bacteria spread into pathogens, treatments fail. questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Soil microorganisms no longer produce any of the antibiotics used today.
Pathogens cannot acquire resistance genes from soil bacteria.
Soil holds ancient resistance genes that can move into pathogens, so tracking that movement matters for medicine.
Resistance genes exist only because humans have used antibiotics in medicine.

questions.explanation: The link is between the origin of antibiotics and the origin of resistance, with gene transfer as the route that turns a soil reservoir into a clinical problem.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says many soil resistance genes are ancient and unrelated to clinical use.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says most current antibiotics were first found in soil microorganisms.
distractor_rationales.B: The text describes exactly that spread as the reason treatments fail.

questions.stimulus: Cement production releases carbon dioxide in two ways: fuel burned to heat kilns and the chemical reaction that converts limestone to clinker. Geopolymer binders avoid the limestone step, using aluminosilicate waste such as fly ash instead. They can cut emissions substantially, but their strength depends on the ash's composition, which varies between power plants, so each batch must be tested.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Cement emissions come only from the fuel used to heat kilns.
Geopolymer binders produce more carbon dioxide than ordinary cement.
Geopolymer binders can cut cement emissions, but variable ash composition means each batch needs testing.
Fly ash has a consistent composition wherever it is produced.

questions.explanation: The passage gives an environmental benefit and a practical constraint, and the constraint is the variability of the waste material.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says they can cut emissions substantially.
distractor_rationales.D: The text says composition varies between power plants.
distractor_rationales.A: The text names two sources: fuel and the limestone reaction.

questions.stimulus: Migrating birds often fly at night and orient partly by stars. Artificial light attracts and disorients them, drawing them toward cities where collisions with glass are common. Turning off upper-floor lights during peak migration nights reduces deaths measurably; one city's program cut recorded collisions at a large tower by more than half during the weeks it operated.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Collisions with glass occur mainly during the day, when birds are active.
Birds migrate only on nights when the stars are hidden by city light.
Reducing night lighting during migration saves birds that are drawn off course by artificial light.
Turning off lights increases the number of birds drawn into cities.

questions.explanation: The causal sequence runs from artificial light to disorientation to collisions, and the city program is the evidence that removing light reduces harm.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says birds orient partly by stars, not that they migrate only when stars are hidden.
distractor_rationales.A: The text links collisions to disorientation at night.
distractor_rationales.D: The program is reported as cutting collisions, not raising them.

questions.stimulus: Maya cities in the seasonal tropics depended on reservoirs that stored rainwater through the dry season. Sediment cores from one reservoir show layers of sand and clay laid down quickly, indicating that the floor was dredged repeatedly. The same cores show later layers of algae and eroded soil, suggesting the system was neglected as droughts intensified.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Reservoir sediments record a history of careful maintenance followed by neglect during worsening drought.
Maya cities relied on rivers rather than stored rainwater.
Algae layers show that the water became cleaner over time.
The reservoir was dredged only once, at the end of its use.

questions.explanation: The core evidence is a change in sediment type, and the interpretation is a change from maintenance to neglect under drought.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says cities depended on reservoirs that stored rainwater.
distractor_rationales.D: Repeated dredging is inferred from repeated layers.
distractor_rationales.C: Algae and eroded soil are offered as signs of neglect and declining water quality.

questions.stimulus: During deep sleep, the brain replays sequences of activity recorded during learning, but faster. This replay occurs alongside slow waves that coordinate the hippocampus and cortex. When researchers disrupted those waves in sleeping volunteers, the volunteers remembered fewer of the word pairs they had studied, even though their total sleep time was unchanged.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Replay during sleep erases the sequences recorded during learning.
Memory depends mainly on how many hours a person sleeps.
Slow-wave activity during sleep helps consolidate what was learned, independent of total sleep time.
The hippocampus is inactive during deep sleep.

questions.explanation: The experiment holds sleep time constant and changes only the waves, which isolates slow-wave activity as the factor that matters.

distractor_rationales.B: The disrupted-wave group remembered less with the same total sleep, so hours alone are not the factor.
distractor_rationales.A: Replay is described as strengthening, not erasing, learned sequences.
distractor_rationales.D: The text says the waves coordinate the hippocampus with the cortex.

questions.stimulus: At deep-sea vents, seawater heated by magma carries dissolved metals and hydrogen sulphide. Where the fluid meets cold seawater, minerals precipitate and build chimneys. Microbes there use chemical energy instead of sunlight, supporting tube worms and crabs. Because similar conditions may exist beneath the ice of other worlds, vents are a target in the search for life beyond Earth.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Tube worms at vents feed directly on sunlight filtered through the water.
Deep-sea vents are formed by cold seawater dissolving minerals.
Vents are studied mainly because they contain no living organisms.
Vent ecosystems run on chemical energy rather than sunlight, which makes them a model for life elsewhere.

questions.explanation: The passage describes a food web founded on chemistry, then draws the astrobiological implication from the possibility of similar conditions elsewhere.

distractor_rationales.B: The fluid is heated by magma, and minerals precipitate when it meets cold water.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says the microbes use chemical energy instead of sunlight.
distractor_rationales.C: The text describes a community of microbes, worms and crabs.

questions.stimulus: Sea ice forms by rejecting salt, which concentrates impurities in narrow brine channels. Microplastics carried north by currents become trapped in those channels, so ice can hold far more particles per liter than the water beneath it. When the ice melts in spring, the particles are released into surface water precisely where plankton bloom.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Sea ice concentrates microplastics and releases them in spring where plankton are blooming.
Sea ice filters microplastics out of the ocean and stores them permanently.
Plankton blooms occur in winter, after the ice has formed.
Microplastics are less concentrated in sea ice than in the water below it.

questions.explanation: Two mechanisms combine: brine channels trap particles, and spring melt releases them at the moment and place where plankton are most active.

distractor_rationales.B: The ice releases the particles when it melts rather than storing them permanently.
distractor_rationales.D: The text says ice can hold far more particles per liter.
distractor_rationales.C: The release is described as happening in spring, when plankton bloom.

questions.stimulus: Wind turbine blades are built from glass fibres set in resin, a composite that is strong and light but hard to separate. Most retired blades are buried or burned. New methods dissolve the resin so the fibres can be reused, or replace it with a thermoplastic that can be melted and remoulded. Each approach must still compete with the low cost of making a new blade.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Thermoplastic resins make blades impossible to remould.
Burying blades is now more expensive than recycling them.
Recycling retired blades is technically possible, but the economics must improve for it to replace disposal.
Turbine blades are made of a single material that is easy to recycle.

questions.explanation: The passage presents two recycling routes and then names cost as the barrier, so the conclusion is technical feasibility with an economic caveat.

distractor_rationales.D: The blades are a composite of glass fibre and resin, which is why separation is difficult.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says recycling must compete with low-cost new blades and does not claim burial is pricier.
distractor_rationales.A: A thermoplastic is described as meltable and remouldable.

questions.stimulus: Romans sweetened wine by boiling it in lead vessels. The resulting syrup was concentrated and sweet, and the lead it picked up was consumed in quantity. Skeletal remains from some Roman sites show elevated lead, though the contribution of any single source is debated. Archaeologists therefore treat sapa as one exposure among several, including water pipes and cosmetics.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Lead-sweetened syrup was a real source of exposure but one of several that archaeologists must weigh together.
Roman wine contained no lead because the vessels were lined with tin.
Skeletal remains show that lead exposure was limited to a single source.
Archaeologists agree that water pipes were the only source of Roman lead exposure.

questions.explanation: The passage accepts the exposure but frames it as one contributor among several whose relative weight remains uncertain.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the syrup picked up lead from the vessels.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says the contribution of any single source is debated.
distractor_rationales.D: Pipes are listed as one of several sources, not the only one.

questions.stimulus: Some orchids produce no nectar but resemble the females of a particular bee species in shape, color and scent. Males attempt to mate with the flower and carry pollen away. The mimicry works only if the orchid is rarer than the bee; when orchids become common, males learn to avoid them and pollination falls. This frequency dependence helps explain why such orchids remain sparse.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The orchids attract bees by offering a large supply of nectar.
Male bees learn to prefer orchids once the flowers become common.
Orchids are abundant because mimicry becomes more effective as they multiply.
Orchid mimicry succeeds only while the flowers stay rarer than the bees they imitate.

questions.explanation: The dependence on relative frequency is the central claim, and it explains the observed scarcity rather than contradicting it.

distractor_rationales.A: The orchids produce no nectar.
distractor_rationales.B: Males learn to avoid the flowers when they become common.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says pollination falls as orchids multiply, which keeps them sparse.

questions.stimulus: People learning a new motor skill improve quickly at first, then plateau, then improve again after a night's sleep. Brain imaging shows that the sleeping brain replays the movement, strengthening the connections that support it. Practising a slightly different version of the movement before sleep can improve the original more than repeating the same movement, a phenomenon called variability training.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Motor learning stops once a person reaches a plateau.
Sleep consolidates motor learning, and varied practice before sleep can strengthen the original skill.
Brain imaging shows no activity related to movement during sleep.
Repeating exactly the same movement is the most effective way to improve it.

questions.explanation: The passage joins a sleep effect to a practice effect: replay during sleep supports consolidation, and variation before sleep appears to enhance it.

distractor_rationales.A: The text says improvement resumes after sleep following a plateau.
distractor_rationales.D: The text reports that a slightly different movement can help more than exact repetition.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says the sleeping brain replays the movement.

questions.stimulus: Mangrove roots slow water and trap sediment, raising the seabed over time. During storms, the dense stems and roots absorb wave energy before it reaches the shore. Studies after cyclones find less damage behind wide mangrove belts than behind cleared shoreline, though a narrow fringe offers little protection against the largest surges.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A narrow fringe of mangroves prevents damage from even the largest surges.
Mangroves increase wave energy by funnelling water toward the shore.
Wide mangrove belts reduce storm damage, though a thin fringe provides little protection.
Mangrove roots prevent sediment from accumulating on the seabed.

questions.explanation: The passage links protection to the width of the belt and explicitly limits what a narrow fringe can do against extreme surges.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the roots absorb wave energy.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says a narrow fringe offers little protection against the largest surges.
distractor_rationales.D: The text says the roots trap sediment and raise the seabed.

questions.stimulus: Tablets from a Mesopotamian archive record grain deliveries, receipts and loans. Because scribes dated many tablets by the regnal year of a king, the archive lets historians reconstruct prices and wages across decades. Some tablets were later reused as filler in walls, and their order in the rubble has to be reconstructed before the records can be read as a series.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Once their order is reconstructed, the tablets yield a long-run economic record.
The archive contains only religious texts with no economic information.
The tablets are useless because they were reused as building material.
Scribes dated tablets by the harvest rather than by a king's reign.

questions.explanation: The value depends on sequence: dating by regnal year plus physical reconstruction turns individual receipts into a series covering decades.

distractor_rationales.C: The reuse is a problem to solve, not a reason the tablets are useless.
distractor_rationales.B: The tablets record deliveries, receipts and loans.
distractor_rationales.D: The text says scribes used the regnal year of a king.

questions.stimulus: Legumes such as clover host bacteria that convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can use. Sowing them between cash crops adds nitrogen to the soil, reducing fertiliser need. But the cover must be killed before it competes with the next crop, and in dry regions it can consume water that the cash crop needs. Farmers therefore choose species and timing by climate.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Water availability has no effect on which cover crop a farmer chooses.
Cover crops remove nitrogen from the soil and increase fertiliser needs.
Cover crops can be left growing through the cash crop without any cost.
Legume cover crops add nitrogen but must be managed for water and competition, so the choice depends on climate.

questions.explanation: The passage sets a benefit against two costs, water use and competition, and concludes that local climate governs the decision.

distractor_rationales.B: The legumes add nitrogen, reducing fertiliser need.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says the cover must be killed before it competes with the next crop.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says farmers choose species and timing by climate, including dryness.

questions.stimulus: A moving bicycle stays upright without a rider. For years the explanation was gyroscopic effect: spinning wheels resist tipping. Experiments with counter-rotating wheels that cancel the gyroscopic effect showed the bicycle still stabilised itself, but only at sufficient speed. Steering geometry that lets the front wheel turn toward a lean turns out to be the key.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A bicycle stabilises itself at any speed, including when stationary.
Counter-rotating wheels make a bicycle more stable than ordinary wheels.
Steering geometry, rather than wheel spin alone, is what keeps a moving bicycle upright.
Gyroscopic effect is the only reason a bicycle stays upright.

questions.explanation: The experiment is designed to eliminate one explanation, and the surviving explanation is the steering geometry that turns the wheel into a lean.

distractor_rationales.D: The counter-rotating experiment removed the gyroscopic effect and the bicycle still stabilised.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says stabilisation requires sufficient speed.
distractor_rationales.B: The counter-rotating wheels canceled the effect, which was done to test, not to improve, stability.

questions.stimulus: Coral fragments grown on underwater frames can be replanted onto damaged reefs. Survival is highest when fragments come from the same reef and are planted in dense clusters, because nearby corals share water flow and can fuse. Restoration is expensive per hectare, however, and cannot offset warming unless the underlying stress is reduced.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Coral restoration can work locally but is costly and cannot substitute for reducing the stress that kills reefs.
Fragments from distant reefs survive better than local fragments.
Planting corals far apart improves their survival.
Restoration alone is enough to offset rising ocean temperatures.

questions.explanation: The passage gives practical conditions for success and then a limit: local replanting does not address the warming that drives loss.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says survival is highest when fragments come from the same reef.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says dense clusters survive best.
distractor_rationales.D: The text says restoration cannot offset warming without reducing the stress.

questions.stimulus: Many vaccines lose potency if they freeze or overheat. In rural clinics without reliable power, keeping them between two and eight degrees is difficult. Solar direct-drive refrigerators use panels and ice banks instead of batteries, so they keep working through cloudy days. Their main constraint is that the panels must be sized for the worst week of the year, not the average.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Solar refrigerators can protect vaccines without reliable power, but they must be sized for the worst conditions.
Panels sized for average conditions are sufficient for a clinic.
Solar refrigerators depend on batteries that fail during cloudy weather.
Vaccines remain effective at any temperature as long as they stay dry.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the design that avoids batteries and then names the sizing rule that makes it reliable in bad weather.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says many vaccines lose potency if they freeze or overheat.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says the units use ice banks instead of batteries.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says panels must be sized for the worst week, not the average.

questions.stimulus: To slow desertification at the edge of dunes, crews set fences of woven reeds perpendicular to the prevailing wind. Sand piles up behind each fence, forming a ridge that stabilises the surface. Once the ridge holds, grasses can be planted, and their roots bind the sand further. The fences themselves decay within a few years, but by then the vegetation has taken over.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Grasses are planted before any sand has accumulated behind the fence.
Fences are built parallel to the wind to spread sand evenly.
Temporary fences create the conditions for vegetation that then stabilises the dune permanently.
Reed fences must be replaced every year to keep a dune stable.

questions.explanation: The sequence is fence, ridge, grass, roots, and the conclusion is that the temporary structure is replaced by a living one.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says the fences decay within a few years and vegetation takes over.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says grasses are planted once the ridge holds.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says the fences are set perpendicular to the prevailing wind.

questions.stimulus: The Bay of Fundy has some of the world's largest tides. Tidal turbines convert the moving water into electricity, but the resource is intermittent in a different way from wind: the tide follows the moon and is predictable decades ahead. Designers can therefore plan output, though the strongest currents last only a few hours around each slack.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The strongest currents at the Bay of Fundy last for most of the day.
Tidal turbines generate electricity only when the tide is slack.
Tidal power is highly predictable but available only in short windows around each tide.
Tidal power is less predictable than wind because the moon's orbit varies.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts predictability with availability: the timing is known far in advance, but the usable current is brief.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says the tide is predictable decades ahead, unlike wind.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says strong currents last only a few hours around each slack.
distractor_rationales.B: The turbines use moving water; slack water is when the current is weakest.

questions.stimulus: Insects colonise a body in a predictable order, and the development of each species depends on temperature. An investigator who knows the temperature history of the site can estimate how long a body has been exposed. The method is most reliable in warm weather and least reliable indoors or in winter, when development slows and the sequence is harder to read.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Cold weather speeds insect development and improves estimates.
The order in which insects arrive is random and cannot be used.
Insect development can estimate time since death, but its accuracy depends on temperature and setting.
Insect evidence is equally reliable indoors and outdoors.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the method through temperature-dependent development and then names the conditions that undermine it.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says the method is least reliable indoors or in winter.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says development slows in winter.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says insects colonise in a predictable order.

questions.stimulus: A concert hall's acoustics depend less on its size than on how quickly sound decays and how it reflects. Surfaces that diffuse sound scatter reflections in many directions, giving the audience a sense of envelopment. A hall designed with too much absorption sounds clear but dry; one with too little sounds muddy. Designers therefore balance reflective and absorptive surfaces carefully.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Good hall acoustics come from balancing reflected and absorbed sound rather than from size alone.
Diffusing surfaces concentrate reflections in a single direction.
Adding as much absorption as possible produces the clearest sound.
Larger halls always sound better than smaller ones.

questions.explanation: The passage rejects size as the main factor and frames design as a balance between two extremes, each with a distinct flaw.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says acoustics depend less on size than on decay and reflection.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says too much absorption leaves a hall dry.
distractor_rationales.B: Diffusing surfaces scatter sound in many directions.

questions.stimulus: A vault in the Arctic permafrost stores seeds at minus eighteen degrees, cold enough to slow ageing for decades. But the vault is a backup, not a working collection: seeds must periodically be grown out to produce fresh, viable samples. The greatest threat to stored seeds is not the cold failing but the samples being too few, so that repeated regeneration narrows their genetic diversity.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The main danger to stored seeds is a failure of the refrigeration.
Repeated regeneration increases the genetic diversity of a sample.
A seed vault preserves samples only if they are periodically regenerated, and small samples lose diversity over time.
The vault keeps seeds alive indefinitely without any need for regeneration.

questions.explanation: The passage corrects a common assumption: the risk is not the freezer but the genetics of a small sample renewed too often.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says seeds must periodically be grown out for fresh samples.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says the greatest threat is too few samples, not the cold failing.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says repeated regeneration narrows diversity.

questions.stimulus: Roman aqueducts ran for tens of kilometres with gradients of only a fraction of a percent. Keeping that slope exact required surveying with levels and cords over difficult ground, and the channels were built with a slight covering to keep out sun and debris. Modern surveys show sections that descend too steeply to have flowed, suggesting some were never completed.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Modern surveys show that every aqueduct section once carried water.
The channels were left open to the sky to keep the water cool.
Roman aqueducts were built with steep gradients to increase water speed.
Aqueducts demanded precise surveying, and some surviving sections suggest unfinished rather than working channels.

questions.explanation: The passage pairs an engineering requirement with physical evidence that not every surviving stretch met it, which changes how those stretches are read.

distractor_rationales.C: The text says gradients were only a fraction of a percent.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says the channels had a covering to keep out sun and debris.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says some sections descend too steeply to have flowed.

questions.stimulus: Streetlights attract insects, and bats that hunt insects gather under them. But some species avoid light, and the ones that tolerate it may arrive late and feed on already-depleted swarms. Surveys along lit and unlit paths find different species compositions, with light-averse bats retreating to dark corridors. Lighting redesign that shields the bulb can reduce the shift.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Insects are repelled by streetlights, leaving bats with less food.
All bat species benefit equally from street lighting.
Shielding a bulb increases the area lit by a streetlight.
Street lighting helps some bats and displaces others, and shielded fixtures can limit the disruption.

questions.explanation: The passage sets a benefit for tolerant bats against a cost for light-averse ones and then names a design change that lessens the divide.

distractor_rationales.B: The text distinguishes tolerant species from light-averse ones.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says lights attract insects.
distractor_rationales.C: Shielding is offered as a way to reduce the ecological shift.

questions.stimulus: Recycled glass melts at a lower temperature than raw materials, so using it saves energy. Contamination by ceramics or heat-resistant glass, however, raises the melting point and can ruin a whole batch. Sorting technology that identifies materials by their optical properties has improved recovery, but collection systems that mix colors still limit what can be remade into new containers.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Glass recycling saves energy, but contamination and mixed colors limit how much can be remade.
Sorting by optical properties has made color mixing unnecessary.
Ceramics lower the melting point and improve the recycling process.
Recycled glass requires more energy to melt than raw materials.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the energy benefit and then two practical limits, one at the material level and one in collection.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says recycled glass melts at a lower temperature.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says ceramics raise the melting point and can ruin a batch.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says mixed colors still limit what can be remade.

questions.stimulus: Seismic waves travel more slowly than the electronic signals that carry a warning. Sensors near an epicentre can detect the first, faster waves and send an alert ahead of the slower, damaging waves. The warning lasts only seconds near the source, but it is enough to stop trains and open fire doors. The system's value depends on dense sensors and fast processing.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The system is valuable mainly because it predicts when an earthquake will occur.
Early warning works by detecting fast waves and outrunning the slower damaging ones, and it depends on sensor density.
The slower waves arrive first and give the system time to react.
Earthquake warnings reach distant cities before they reach nearby towns.

questions.explanation: The mechanism is a race between wave speeds, and the practical value depends on detecting the first waves quickly and processing them fast.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says warnings last only seconds near the source.
distractor_rationales.C: The faster waves arrive first and trigger the alert before the damaging waves.
distractor_rationales.A: The text does not claim prediction of earthquakes, only warning after they begin.

questions.stimulus: Lichen absorbs water and nutrients directly through its surface, so it accumulates airborne elements rather than filtering them. Surveys find that lichen communities near smelters are dominated by a few tolerant species, while sensitive species disappear. Researchers sampling lichen tissue at various distances from a smelter found metal concentrations declining with distance. This pattern suggests that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the composition of a lichen community can serve as a measure of airborne metal pollution
lichen grows faster near smelters because metals are nutrients
sensitive lichen species are more tolerant of pollution than dominant ones
airborne metals are deposited evenly at every distance from a smelter

questions.explanation: Tissue concentrations and species composition both change with distance from the source, so the community itself records the exposure.

distractor_rationales.B: The sensitive species disappear near smelters, which does not suggest faster growth.
distractor_rationales.C: The text calls the sensitive species sensitive and the survivors tolerant.
distractor_rationales.D: The measurements show a decline with distance, not even deposition.

questions.stimulus: Prairie voles form lasting pairs, and their brains release oxytocin when they are together. Blocking oxytocin receptors prevents pair formation, while boosting them speeds it. In a related species that does not form pairs, the same receptors are distributed differently in the brain. These findings indicate that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: where oxytocin receptors sit in the brain may matter as much as whether they are present
oxytocin prevents pair formation in all rodent species
