distractor_rationales.D: The passage says estimates do not transfer between sites.

questions.stimulus: A star catalog is a snapshot that ages. Stars move, and a position recorded with great precision in one decade can be wrong by a noticeable margin a century later. Astronomers therefore re-measure reference stars to track proper motion, the slow drift across the sky. Older catalogues remain useful not despite their age but because of it: the long interval between observations is what makes the drift visible.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Astronomers measure proper motion by observing a star only once.
Old star catalogues gain value from their age, because the time gap reveals how stars have moved.
Stars hold fixed positions, so old catalogues remain accurate indefinitely.
Proper motion makes historical catalogues useless for modern astronomy.

questions.explanation: The passage explains drift, the need for re-measurement, and the special value of long time baselines.

distractor_rationales.C: The text says positions drift over time.
distractor_rationales.D: Old catalogues are described as useful precisely because of their age.
distractor_rationales.A: Motion requires comparison across observations.

questions.stimulus: Inca suspension bridges were woven from grass rope and rebuilt every year. The span was anchored to stone abutments on each bank, and the cables were kept taut by tension applied at the anchors rather than by mid-span supports. Because the material degraded in rain and sun, annual renewal was part of the design, not a repair. The bridge existed as a repeated event rather than as a permanent object.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The bridges were permanent structures rebuilt only after accidents.
The bridges were made from rope that did not degrade in weather.
Annual rebuilding was integral to how these grass-rope bridges worked, not a failure of maintenance.
Stone abutments supported the middle of each span.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the structure and concludes that renewal belonged to the design.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the material degraded in rain and sun.
distractor_rationales.D: The abutments anchored the ends; there were no mid-span supports.
distractor_rationales.A: Renewal was annual and planned, not a response to accidents.

questions.stimulus: Honey crystallises because it is a supersaturated sugar solution. Glucose comes out of solution first, forming small crystals; the rest of the honey then sets around them. Gentle warming redissolves the crystals, but overheating destroys the enzymes that make honey distinctive. Whether a jar crystallises quickly depends mostly on its ratio of glucose to fructose, which varies with the flowers the bees visited.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The glucose-to-fructose ratio is identical in every jar of honey.
Crystallisation is a natural consequence of honey's sugar balance and can be reversed without overheating.
Heating honey strongly is the recommended way to restore it.
Crystallisation indicates that honey has begun to spoil.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the chemistry, the safe remedy, and the floral source of variation.

distractor_rationales.D: The passage treats crystallisation as physical, not spoilage.
distractor_rationales.C: Overheating destroys enzymes, so strong heat is not recommended.
distractor_rationales.A: The ratio varies with the flowers visited.

questions.stimulus: Rock art is hard to photograph without flattening it. A camera pointed straight at a carved panel loses the shadows that make the figures legible. Photogrammetry solves this by taking many overlapping images from different angles and rebuilding the surface as a three-dimensional model. Light can then be aimed across the digital surface from any direction, revealing carving depth that no single photograph recorded.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Photogrammetry requires a single photograph taken in flat light.
Carved panels are easier to read in photographs than in person.
Photogrammetry preserves the surface relief of rock art that ordinary photographs flatten.
The digital model removes the need to record the site at all.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts flat photography with multi-angle reconstruction and explains the advantage of relighting the model.

distractor_rationales.A: The method uses many overlapping images.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says photographs lose the shadows that make figures legible.
distractor_rationales.D: The model is a record of the site, not a replacement for recording.

questions.stimulus: A fish ladder is a staircase of small pools built around a dam. Each pool is low enough for a fish to jump or swim into, and the flow between pools is kept slow enough that the animal is not swept back. Designs differ by species: a ladder tuned for salmon, which leap, may be unusable for bottom-dwelling fish that cannot clear a step at all.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Fish ladders are built to speed water past a dam rather than to help fish.
A single ladder design works for every species in a river.
Fish ladders must be designed for the swimming and jumping abilities of the species that need them.
Bottom-dwelling fish pass ladders more easily than salmon do.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the pool staircase and explains why a design suited to jumpers can fail other species.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says designs differ by species.
distractor_rationales.A: The pools are built to let fish ascend.
distractor_rationales.D: Bottom-dwelling fish may be unable to clear a step.

questions.stimulus: Adobe walls stay comfortable in hot, dry climates because they combine mass with delay. During the day the wall absorbs heat slowly; by the time that heat reaches the interior, the outside air has cooled. Thick walls work because the delay is long, not because the material insulates especially well. In humid climates the same walls can trap moisture, which is why the technique spread most widely in dry regions.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Adobe construction performs best in humid regions.
Adobe's comfort comes from the delay created by wall mass, which suits dry climates better than humid ones.
Adobe walls cool a room by insulating it almost perfectly.
Thin adobe walls are more effective than thick ones in hot climates.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the thermal delay and ties the technique's distribution to dry climates.

distractor_rationales.C: The text says the delay, not insulation, is the key.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage credits thick walls with a longer delay.
distractor_rationales.A: Humid climates can trap moisture in adobe.

questions.stimulus: Some seeds germinate only after fire. Their coats are impermeable to water until heat cracks them, and some species also respond to chemicals in smoke. This delays germination until a fire has cleared competing vegetation and returned nutrients to the soil. A seed that sprouted immediately would face shade and competition; waiting is an advantage, not a delay.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Fire destroys the seed coats of every species in a burned area.
Smoke chemicals prevent seeds from germinating after a fire.
Seeds that germinate immediately gain an advantage over fire-followers.
Fire-triggered germination is advantageous because it times sprouting to conditions after a fire.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the mechanism and the benefit of timing germination to post-fire conditions.

distractor_rationales.A: The text describes some seeds, not every species.
distractor_rationales.B: Smoke chemicals can trigger germination.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says waiting avoids shade and competition.

questions.stimulus: Corten steel is formulated to rust in a controlled way. Its alloying elements form a dense, adherent oxide layer on the surface, which then slows further corrosion. Ordinary steel rusts through because its oxide flakes away and exposes fresh metal. Corten therefore needs the right cycle of wetting and drying to develop its protective skin; in constant damp or in salt air the layer may never stabilise.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Corten steel never corrodes at all because it contains no iron.
Corten steel resists corrosion by forming a stable oxide layer, but only under suitable weathering conditions.
Corten performs best where surfaces stay constantly wet.
Ordinary steel forms a tighter oxide layer than corten steel does.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts corten with ordinary steel and names the wetting cycle needed for the protective layer.

distractor_rationales.A: The text describes controlled rusting, not immunity to corrosion.
distractor_rationales.D: Ordinary steel's oxide flakes away.
distractor_rationales.C: Constant damp can prevent the layer from stabilising.

questions.stimulus: Glass must be cooled slowly after shaping. Rapid cooling sets the outside while the inside is still contracting, which leaves stresses locked in the object. An annealing oven holds the piece just below its softening point and then lowers the temperature over hours, letting the interior catch up. Skip that step and a bowl may shatter weeks later, long after it has left the workshop.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Glass that cools too quickly fails immediately, never later.
Slow, controlled cooling prevents the internal stresses that make glass fail later.
Annealing raises glass above its softening point and holds it there.
Rapid cooling strengthens glass by locking the outside in compression.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the stress created by fast cooling and the schedule that avoids it.

distractor_rationales.D: The passage presents rapid cooling as the cause of failure.
distractor_rationales.C: Annealing holds the piece just below the softening point.
distractor_rationales.A: The text says a bowl may shatter weeks later.

questions.stimulus: Tardigrades survive desiccation by replacing most of their body water with a sugar that turns their cells into a glass-like state. Metabolism stops, membranes hold their shape, and the animal can revive when water returns. The trick is not unique to tardigrades, but their version is unusually effective. What the sugar does is physical rather than chemical: it immobilises molecules so they cannot react or unfold.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The protective sugar works through a chemical reaction that repairs DNA.
Only tardigrades possess any mechanism for surviving desiccation.
A glass-forming sugar protects tardigrades during drought by physically immobilising their cells.
Tardigrades survive drought by keeping their normal metabolism running.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the dried state and explains the physical protective role of the sugar.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says metabolism stops.
distractor_rationales.A: The passage calls the effect physical, not chemical.
distractor_rationales.B: The trick is not unique to tardigrades.

questions.stimulus: Fog-collecting nets work because droplets in fog are large enough to strike mesh fibres and coalesce. The water then runs down the strands into a trough. Fine mesh catches more droplets but clogs with dust, while coarse mesh sheds water well but misses much of it. Designers therefore tune mesh density to the local fog, which is why installations from different coastal deserts look so unlike one another.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Fine mesh always outperforms coarse mesh in every climate.
Fog nets must be tuned to local conditions because mesh density trades capture against clogging.
Mesh density has no effect on how much water a net gathers.
Fog nets collect water by condensing vapour inside a tank.

questions.explanation: The passage explains droplet capture and the competing costs of mesh density, then links design differences to local fog.

distractor_rationales.A: Fine mesh clogs with dust, so it is not always better.
distractor_rationales.D: Collection relies on droplets striking mesh, not a tank.
distractor_rationales.C: Density is described as the key trade-off.

questions.stimulus: City trees cool streets in two ways: they cast shade and they release water vapour through their leaves. Shade acts immediately on surfaces below the canopy, while evaporation lowers air temperature more gradually. A single young tree does little of either, and a row of trees in sealed pavement may never reach the size needed. Cooling benefits therefore depend on long-term growth as much as on planting.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Trees cool streets only by casting shade, with no evaporative effect.
Sealed pavement helps street trees reach full size faster.
Young trees provide more cooling than mature ones.
Urban tree cooling depends on the trees surviving and growing large, not only on how many are planted.

questions.explanation: The passage presents the two cooling mechanisms and stresses that benefit grows with the tree.

distractor_rationales.A: The passage names evaporation as a second mechanism.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says a young tree does little.
distractor_rationales.B: Sealed pavement is described as a barrier to growth.

questions.stimulus: Krill gather in swarms so dense that sonar can mistake them for the seabed. The swarm is not a herd in the usual sense: individuals do not follow a leader but adjust to neighbors, and the group darkens as it thickens, which may confuse predators. Because swarms shift shape quickly, surveys that sample one patch may badly misestimate the population of a whole region.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Krill swarms form through local interactions and move in ways that make population surveys hard.
Krill swarms are led by a single dominant individual.
Sonar accurately counts krill because swarms scatter sound weakly.
Krill swarms keep a fixed shape throughout the day.

questions.explanation: The passage explains neighbor-based grouping, the effect on predators, and the difficulty for surveys.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says individuals adjust to neighbors, not a leader.
distractor_rationales.C: Sonar can mistake swarms for the seabed, which is not accuracy.
distractor_rationales.D: The swarms shift shape quickly.

questions.stimulus: A lightning rod does not attract lightning from a distance. It provides a low-resistance path from roof to ground, so that a strike arriving nearby passes through metal instead of through timber. The sharp tip matters less than the continuous connection: a rod with a broken conductor is worse than none, because it invites a discharge it cannot carry away.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A lightning rod pulls strikes toward a building from far away.
The sharpness of the tip is the only feature that provides protection.
A rod with a broken conductor still protects the structure.
A lightning rod protects a building by giving current a continuous path to the ground.

questions.explanation: The passage defines the rod's job as a conductive path and stresses that the path must be unbroken.

distractor_rationales.A: The text denies that the rod attracts lightning from a distance.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says the continuous connection matters more than the tip.
distractor_rationales.C: A broken conductor is described as worse than no rod.

questions.stimulus: Every flat map distorts something. Mercator preserves direction, which is why it suited navigation, but it stretches area toward the poles so that Greenland appears larger than Africa. A projection that preserves area must give up shape, and one that preserves shape must give up area. The choice is not a matter of accuracy but of which property a particular map is meant to show.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Mercator is the only projection that preserves true area.
It is possible to preserve area, shape and direction on one flat map.
Greenland is in fact larger in area than Africa.
Map projections trade one geometric property for another, so the right map depends on its purpose.

questions.explanation: The passage names the trade-offs and concludes that purpose determines the choice.

distractor_rationales.A: Mercator preserves direction and stretches area.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says preserving one property requires giving up another.
distractor_rationales.C: The text uses Greenland's apparent size as an example of distortion.

questions.stimulus: A camel's hump stores fat, not water. Burning that fat releases energy and also produces water as a by-product, which helps in dry conditions. Concentrating the store on the back also keeps the animal cooler than an even layer of fat would, since heat can escape from the rest of the body. The hump therefore serves both as fuel reserve and as a way of managing heat.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Burning fat consumes water rather than producing it.
Fat spread evenly over the body would keep a camel cooler.
The hump stores energy and helps regulate heat, rather than holding water directly.
The hump is a sac of liquid water carried for long journeys.

questions.explanation: The passage corrects the water myth and explains both the energy and heat-management roles.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says the hump stores fat, not water.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says an even layer would be less cool.
distractor_rationales.A: Burning fat produces water as a by-product.

questions.stimulus: An octopus changes color by stretching pigment sacs in its skin. Muscles pull each sac open or closed, so the change is under direct neural control and can happen in under a second. The skin also carries reflective cells that scatter light, which lets the animal match a surface even when its pigments alone could not. Color change is therefore both fast and structural.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Octopus color change is fast because it is muscular and structural rather than chemical.
The pigment sacs cannot be controlled by the animal.
Octopuses change color slowly as pigments are produced chemically.
Reflective cells prevent the skin from matching a surface.

questions.explanation: The passage describes muscular pigment sacs and reflective cells and concludes that the mechanism is fast and structural.

distractor_rationales.C: The text says the change takes under a second and is neural.
distractor_rationales.D: Reflective cells help the match.
distractor_rationales.B: Muscles under neural control open and close the sacs.

questions.stimulus: A vaccine that leaves the factory must stay cold all the way to the clinic. Each transfer between a refrigerator, a vehicle and a field cooler is a chance for the chain to break. Health programs therefore attach temperature indicators to every box and train staff to reject a shipment whose indicator has changed, even if the vials look normal. The vial itself gives no warning.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Because spoiled vaccine may look unchanged, programs rely on temperature indicators and strict handling rules.
Staff can tell a spoiled shipment by inspecting the vials.
Temperature indicators are attached only after a shipment reaches a clinic.
Vaccines remain effective after any number of breaks in the cold chain.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the fragile chain and the visual check that replaces inspecting the vials.

distractor_rationales.D: The text treats each transfer as a risk.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says the vial gives no warning.
distractor_rationales.C: Indicators are attached to every box before transit.

questions.stimulus: Mangrove seedlings are planted in mud that shifts with every tide. A propagule pushed into soft sediment may be washed out before its roots take hold, so planters often use bamboo stakes or biodegradable anchors. Survival also depends on hydrology: seedlings placed too low are flooded too often, while those placed too high dry out. Successful restoration is therefore a matter of choosing the right elevation as much as planting.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Mangrove seedlings survive equally well at any height above the tide line.
Mangrove restoration succeeds only when seedlings are anchored and planted at the right tidal elevation.
Planting alone is enough, regardless of where seedlings are placed.
Bamboo stakes are used to raise seedlings above the reach of tides.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the two risks, anchoring and elevation, and concludes that placement matters as much as planting.

distractor_rationales.A: The text says elevation determines flooding and drying.
distractor_rationales.D: Stakes anchor seedlings in soft mud; they do not raise them.
distractor_rationales.C: Placement is described as decisive.

questions.stimulus: Desert varnish is a thin dark coating that accumulates on stable rock surfaces over thousands of years. It forms as wind-blown clay and microbes deposit manganese and iron oxides. Because the coating builds slowly and only where rock stays undisturbed, archaeologists use its thickness and chemistry to estimate how long a surface has been exposed. A varnish date is a minimum age for the carving beneath it.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The coating is composed mainly of organic material from plants.
Varnish dates give the exact year a carving was made.
Desert varnish accumulates slowly on undisturbed rock and can give a minimum age for carvings.
Desert varnish forms quickly wherever rock is exposed to rain.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the slow formation and the cautious minimum-age interpretation.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says it accumulates over thousands of years.
distractor_rationales.B: It provides a minimum age, not an exact year.
distractor_rationales.A: The coating is clay plus manganese and iron oxides.

questions.stimulus: An ancient stone amphitheatre can carry a whisper from the stage to the highest tier. The curved wall reflects sound back toward the center, and the seating steps scatter it so that it arrives with little delay. Modern concrete halls often need amplification because their flat surfaces absorb or diffuse energy. The old design worked with geometry rather than with power.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The amphitheatre's curved geometry carried sound effectively without electronic amplification.
Flat modern surfaces reflect sound more efficiently than curved ones.
Ancient amphitheatres relied on hidden amplification devices.
The seating steps absorbed sound before it reached the upper tiers.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts curved stone geometry with flat modern surfaces and notes that the old design needed no power.

distractor_rationales.C: No amplification is described; geometry does the work.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says flat surfaces absorb or diffuse energy.
distractor_rationales.D: The steps scatter sound so it arrives with little delay.

questions.stimulus: A pollinator strip is a band of flowers sown along a field edge. It offers nectar and pollen through the season, so bees and hoverflies remain nearby instead of dispersing. Studies find more pollinators inside adjacent crops, though the effect depends on which flowers are sown and on whether pesticides drift onto the strip. A strip that blooms for two weeks helps far less than one that flowers across the growing season.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Pollinator strips can support nearby crops, but their benefit depends on duration and on how they are managed.
Pollinator strips work best when they bloom for only a short period.
Pesticide drift improves the value of a pollinator strip.
Any flower strip guarantees a larger harvest in the adjacent field.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the mechanism, notes the conditional benefits, and contrasts short and long blooming.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says the effect depends on species and pesticide drift.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says a long flowering season helps more.
distractor_rationales.C: Drift is named as a factor that can reduce the benefit.

questions.stimulus: Newsprint made before the 1870s was manufactured from rags and remains flexible. Later papers used groundwood pulp, which retains lignin and turns brittle as it oxidises. A single brittle volume can crack its neighbors as it is shelved and pulled. Conservators therefore box each fragile item separately, slowing the transfer of acid and preventing mechanical damage from the book beside it.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Lignin-rich paper becomes brittle, so fragile volumes are boxed separately to prevent damage to neighbors.
Rag paper turns brittle faster than groundwood paper.
Lignin makes paper more flexible as it ages.
Boxing a volume increases the acid it transfers to its neighbors.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the two papers and explains why separate boxes protect a collection.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says rag paper remains flexible.
distractor_rationales.D: Boxing slows acid transfer rather than increasing it.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says lignin-bearing paper turns brittle.

questions.stimulus: A tidal turbine blade works in water far denser than air, so the same diameter extracts far more power than a wind turbine's. That density also loads the blade heavily and wears its leading edge, and salt water corrodes fittings that would last decades in air. Designs therefore favor thick, simple sections that tolerate abrasion rather than the slender aerofoils used on wind farms.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Tidal turbines produce less power than wind turbines of the same diameter.
Tidal turbines gain power from dense water but must be built more ruggedly than wind turbines.
Slender aerofoil sections are preferred for tidal blades.
Salt water protects tidal turbine fittings from corrosion.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the power advantage and the wear and corrosion penalties that shape the design.

distractor_rationales.A: The text says dense water yields far more power.
distractor_rationales.D: Salt water is described as corrosive.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says tidal designs favor thick sections.

questions.stimulus: Coffee beans crack audibly twice during roasting. The first crack marks the point at which water and gases force their way out of the bean; the second comes later as the structure begins to fracture. Roasters listen for these sounds because they mark stages that are hard to judge by color alone. A bean pulled at the first crack tastes quite different from one taken past the second.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The two cracking sounds give roasters reliable markers for stages that color alone cannot show.
Beans taken at the first and second cracks taste the same.
Coffee beans crack only once, at the very end of roasting.
Roasters rely on color because the cracks are inaudible.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the physical cause of each crack and explains why roasters use them.

distractor_rationales.C: The text describes two distinct cracks.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage says the cracks mark stages hard to judge by color.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says the flavours differ.

questions.stimulus: Banknote paper is made from cotton and linen fibres rather than wood pulp. The long fibres flex without tearing, and the sheet is sized so that ink sits on the surface instead of soaking through. A watermark is formed during manufacture by pressing the wet sheet against a shaped mould, which thins the paper in a pattern that becomes visible when held to light. The security feature is part of the sheet, not printed on it.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Durable fibres and a watermark formed within the sheet make banknote paper hard to copy.
Banknote paper is made from wood pulp for extra stiffness.
Short fibres make banknote paper more resistant to tearing.
The watermark is printed onto the finished sheet with ink.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the fibre choice, the sizing, and the in-sheet watermark that makes the note hard to forge.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says cotton and linen, not wood pulp.
distractor_rationales.D: The watermark is formed during manufacture, not printed.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage attributes durability to long fibres.

questions.stimulus: A museum's climate system is designed around slow change rather than constant conditions. Materials such as wood and ivory expand and contract as humidity shifts, and repeated cycling does more damage than a steady level slightly outside the ideal range. Curators therefore accept small departures from the target if the readings stay stable, and they watch the rate of change as closely as the value itself.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The rate of change is irrelevant if the average value is correct.
Museums should keep every gallery at the exact ideal humidity at all times.
Wood and ivory are unaffected by changes in humidity.
Stable conditions matter more than hitting an exact target, because repeated swings damage objects.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts cycling with stability and concludes that rate of change is a key measure.

distractor_rationales.B: The text accepts small departures when readings are stable.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says such materials expand and contract.
distractor_rationales.A: Curators watch the rate of change closely.

questions.stimulus: A traditional windmill's sails turn a central shaft that drives millstones through gears. The stones must turn at a steady speed: too fast and the flour heats and loses quality, too slow and the grain is not cut cleanly. Millers therefore adjust the gap between the stones and the amount of sail cloth according to the wind, a constant negotiation between power and control.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Sail cloth is fixed and never adjusted by the miller.
Millstones work best when they turn as fast as the wind allows.
A miller's work is a continual adjustment of gearing and sail area to keep the stones turning at the right speed.
The gap between the stones has no effect on the flour.

questions.explanation: The passage explains why steady speed matters and names the two controls a miller uses.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says too fast heats the flour and loses quality.
distractor_rationales.D: The gap is one of the two adjustments described.
distractor_rationales.A: Millers adjust sail cloth according to the wind.

questions.stimulus: A cathedral's stained glass looks dull from outside because the colored glass is translucent, not reflective. The design assumes light passing through from behind, so the images face inward. On an overcast day the effect weakens, and on a bright day the leading between panes throws dark lines across the figures. The window is therefore a device for shaping transmitted light rather than a painted surface.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Stained glass is designed for transmitted light, which is why it looks different from outside or under changing skies.
Stained glass is painted to be read by reflected light from outside.
Overcast weather makes the images brighter and sharper.
The leading between panes has no visual effect on the figures.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the transmission model and the visible consequences of weather and leading.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the glass is translucent and lit from behind.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says the effect weakens on overcast days.
distractor_rationales.D: Leading throws dark lines across the figures.

questions.stimulus: An arch carries load by compression. Each stone pushes against its neighbors, and the whole curve transfers the weight outward to the supports. Because stone is strong in compression but weak in tension, an arch needs thick abutments to resist that outward push. A crack at the crown often signals that the supports have spread rather than that the stones themselves have failed.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: An arch carries load mainly through tension in its stones.
Thin abutments are sufficient because the arch pushes inward.
An arch works through compression and needs strong abutments to resist the outward thrust.
A crack at the crown always means the stones have failed.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the compressive path and interprets crown cracks as a sign of support movement.

distractor_rationales.A: The text says load travels by compression.
distractor_rationales.B: The arch pushes outward, so thick abutments are needed.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage says such a crack often indicates spreading supports.

questions.stimulus: The first public aquariums were built as windows into the sea, but the water inside them quickly went stale. Early keepers learned that a tank needs circulation, light and plants to stay clear, and that a closed system collapses without them. Modern aquariums still depend on the same three elements, though they now add filters and chillers. The biology has not changed, only the machinery.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Aquarium keeping depends on circulation, light and plants, and modern equipment only refines those basics.
Modern aquariums no longer need plants or light.
Water in an aquarium improves when it is kept still.
Early aquariums stayed clear because they were sealed off from air.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the early failures and the enduring requirements, noting that technology changed but biology did not.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says closed systems collapse.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says the same three elements remain necessary.
distractor_rationales.C: Circulation is one of the requirements.

questions.stimulus: A weather station in a city park records warmer nights than one at the airport outside town. The difference is the urban heat island: buildings and roads release heat stored during the day, and the city's rough surfaces trap it. The effect is strongest on clear, still nights, when rural ground radiates heat freely to the sky. On windy nights the two stations converge.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Windy nights produce the largest urban-rural temperature gap.
Cities are always cooler than rural areas at night.
Airport stations record the heat island more strongly than park stations.
Cities stay warmer than surrounding land mainly on clear, still nights, because built surfaces release and trap heat.

questions.explanation: The passage defines the heat island and explains why it peaks under clear, calm conditions.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the city park records warmer nights.
distractor_rationales.A: The passage says the effect is strongest on still nights.
distractor_rationales.C: The park station shows the warmer reading.

questions.stimulus: A hand saw cuts on the forward stroke because its teeth are set to lift waste clear of the kerf. Pushing the saw back does little cutting; the return stroke only repositions the blade. Sawyers therefore apply pressure on the push and relax on the return, letting the tool do the work. A saw used with even pressure both ways dulls faster and wanders from the line.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Teeth set to lift waste make the saw dull more slowly.
A hand saw is designed to cut on one stroke, so even pressure in both directions is wasteful and less accurate.
Applying pressure on the return stroke keeps the blade on line.
A hand saw cuts equally well on the forward and return strokes.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the tooth set and the correct stroke, then describes the consequences of ignoring it.

distractor_rationales.D: The text says the return stroke does little cutting.
distractor_rationales.A: No such claim is made about wear and the tooth set.
distractor_rationales.C: Even pressure both ways makes the saw wander.

questions.stimulus: A lighthouse lens does not need to be large to be seen far away. A Fresnel design rings a small central lens with concentric prisms, each bending light from the lamp into a narrow horizontal beam. The result is the reach of a much larger lens at a fraction of the weight and cost. The principle is still used in solar concentrators and in some vehicle lights.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Fresnel lenses work by absorbing light from the lamp and re-emitting it.
A large solid lens is cheaper to make than a Fresnel lens.
The Fresnel design was abandoned and is no longer used.
The Fresnel lens achieves long-range beams with a compact, light assembly.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the prism rings and their advantage in reach, weight and cost.

distractor_rationales.A: The prisms bend light; absorption is not the mechanism.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says the design costs a fraction of a larger lens.
distractor_rationales.C: The principle is still used today.

questions.stimulus: A salt flat looks empty but records water. As a shallow brine pool dries, minerals crystallise in a sequence determined by their solubility, leaving rings of different salts. A core through the crust therefore preserves a history of wet and dry periods. Interpreting that history requires care, because later floods can dissolve and redeposit the very layers a reader hopes to date.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Minerals crystallise in a random order unrelated to solubility.
Salt flats contain no evidence of past water.
Salt crusts record wet and dry periods in layers, though later floods can disturb the record.
Later floods make the layers easier to date.

questions.explanation: The passage explains the layered record and the disturbance that limits interpretation.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the flat records water history.
distractor_rationales.A: The sequence is determined by solubility.
distractor_rationales.D: Floods can dissolve and redeposit layers, complicating dating.

questions.stimulus: A violin's soundpost is a small dowel wedged between the front and back plates inside the instrument. It is not glued; friction and the curve of the plates hold it in place. Moving it a millimetre changes how the instrument responds, which is why players guard it carefully. The post transfers vibration between the plates, and a loose post can make an otherwise healthy violin sound thin.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The soundpost is glued in place so that it cannot move.
A loose soundpost improves the tone of a violin.
Its exact position has little effect on the instrument's sound.
The soundpost is a precisely placed, unglued brace whose position and fit strongly affect a violin's sound.

questions.explanation: The passage describes the post's placement and its role in transferring vibration.

distractor_rationales.A: The text says it is not glued.
distractor_rationales.C: A millimetre of movement changes the response.
distractor_rationales.B: A loose post can make the violin sound thin.

questions.stimulus: Antarctic sponges grow extremely slowly, adding only a fraction of a millimetre each year. A specimen collected at 200 meters had growth bands that took decades to form. Because the bands record the chemistry of the water in which they formed, a single large sponge can preserve a record of changing ocean conditions stretching back further than most instrument series.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Growth bands are unrelated to the chemistry of the surrounding water.
Instrument series are always longer than a sponge's growth record.
Antarctic sponges grow quickly enough to record daily changes in seawater.
Old sponges can serve as archives of ocean chemistry that predate modern measurements.

questions.explanation: Slow growth plus chemistry-bearing bands means a long, pre-instrument archive.

distractor_rationales.C: The text describes growth as extremely slow.
distractor_rationales.A: The bands are said to record water chemistry.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says the sponge record stretches back further.

questions.stimulus: A Roman water wheel recovered from a riverbed had wooden paddles worn thin on one face only. The wear pattern matches contact with flowing water rather than with sand or gravel. The wheel's axle showed no sign of having been turned by an animal. Together these details suggest that the wheel was driven by the current itself.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The wear on the paddles came from abrasive gravel in the riverbed.
The wheel was turned by oxen walking on a circular track.
The wheel was never used and was abandoned before installation.
The wheel was a water-powered device rather than one turned by animals or people.

questions.explanation: The evidence points to current-driven rotation and away from animal power or abrasion.

distractor_rationales.B: The axle shows no animal-drive wear.
distractor_rationales.A: The wear matches flowing water, not sand or gravel.
distractor_rationales.C: Use is implied by the wear pattern.

questions.stimulus: Bats emit calls at frequencies too high for most people to hear. A detector that records ultrasound can therefore reveal species that mist-netting misses, because nets catch only animals flying at net height. In one survey, detectors registered eight species at a site where nets had caught three. The two methods were not measuring the same thing.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The survey proved that only three species live at the site.
Acoustic detectors capture bats physically for identification.
Combining acoustic detectors with nets gives a fuller species list than either method alone.
Mist-netting is more reliable than acoustic detection for every species.

questions.explanation: Each method samples differently, so the union is more complete than either alone.

distractor_rationales.D: Nets missed five species the detectors found.
distractor_rationales.B: Detectors record sound; nets catch animals.
distractor_rationales.A: The detectors found eight species, so three is incomplete.

questions.stimulus: Legumes host bacteria in root nodules that convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use. A field planted with legumes for one season contains more available nitrogen the following year, even after the plants are harvested. Farmers who rotate legumes with cereals often reduce their fertiliser use without lowering yields.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The nitrogen fixed by legumes remains in the soil and benefits the next crop.
Root-nodule bacteria convert nitrogen into a gas that plants cannot use.
Cereal yields fall whenever legumes are grown in rotation.
Legumes remove nitrogen from the soil and deplete it for later crops.

questions.explanation: The rotation effect follows from fixed nitrogen remaining available to the following crop.

distractor_rationales.D: The passage says available nitrogen increases.
distractor_rationales.C: Yields are maintained while fertiliser falls.
distractor_rationales.B: The bacteria produce a usable form.

questions.stimulus: Lighthouse keepers recorded weather every few hours for over a century. Their logs note wind direction, cloud cover and the first appearance of ice. Historians comparing these entries with ships' logs from the same waters find close agreement on storms but frequent disagreement on calm days. The keepers' records are therefore most valuable for severe weather.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The keepers' logs should be discarded because they disagree with ships' logs.
Ships' logs are unreliable because they were written at sea.
The logs are most trustworthy where independent records confirm them, especially during storms.
Calm days are the best evidence of the keepers' accuracy.

questions.explanation: Agreement during storms supports using the logs for severe weather, not for calm conditions.

distractor_rationales.A: Agreement on storms makes the logs useful there.
distractor_rationales.D: Disagreement is most frequent on calm days.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage does not accuse ships' logs of unreliability.

questions.stimulus: Paper marbling floats pigments on a thickened bath, then lays paper on the surface to lift the pattern. Because the bath is viscous, the colors move slowly and can be combed before printing. Two sheets made minutes apart from the same bath differ, since each lift removes pigment. No two marbled sheets are identical.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The combing step prevents any pattern from forming.
Each print is unique because lifting the paper removes pigment from the bath.
Marbled sheets are identical because the bath is stirred between prints.
Pigments sink immediately in the thickened bath.

questions.explanation: Depletion of pigment at each lift explains the uniqueness of every sheet.

distractor_rationales.C: The passage says each lift removes pigment and changes the pattern.
distractor_rationales.D: The viscous bath slows movement rather than sinking.
distractor_rationales.A: Combing shapes the pattern before printing.

questions.stimulus: A lake core contains a thin, pale layer of volcanic ash between darker organic sediment. The ash layer is the same thickness at both ends of the lake, which is unusual for sediment that normally thins away from shore. Geologists conclude that the ash fell directly onto the lake surface across its whole extent in a very short interval.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The layer records a single airborne deposit rather than material washed in from the shore.
The lake was dry when the ash fell.
The layer was deposited by a river entering the lake.
The ash drifted in slowly from one shoreline over many years.

questions.explanation: Uniform thickness across the basin points to airborne deposition over a short time.

distractor_rationales.D: A direct fall explains uniform thickness across the lake.
distractor_rationales.C: River input would thin away from the inlet.
distractor_rationales.B: A dry lake would not preserve an even layer in sediment.

questions.stimulus: Nest temperature determines the sex of some turtle hatchlings. On beaches where shade from vegetation has increased, nests stay cooler and produce more males. Conservationists who move nests to open sand to protect them from tides may unintentionally raise temperatures. Protection and sex ratio can therefore pull in opposite directions.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Moving nests to open sand guarantees a balanced sex ratio.
Shade has no effect on hatchling sex.
Tides are the only threat to nests on shaded beaches.
A nest-relocation program should consider temperature as well as protection from tides.

questions.explanation: The two goals conflict, so relocation must account for both.

distractor_rationales.A: Open sand is warmer, which skews the ratio.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says temperature determines sex.
distractor_rationales.C: The text mentions vegetation and temperature, not only tides.

questions.stimulus: Iron-gall ink etches paper as it ages because it releases acid. A manuscript written in the fifteenth century may have holes where the ink was thickest, even though the surrounding paper is sound. Conservators treat such leaves cautiously: washing removes acid but can also loosen the remaining ink, so a treatment that helps the paper may erase the text.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Preservation choices must balance saving the paper against losing the writing on it.
Holes appear where the ink was thinnest.
Washing always restores both the paper and the ink.
Iron-gall ink strengthens paper where it is applied.

questions.explanation: The risk of losing ink sets a limit on acid removal.

distractor_rationales.C: Washing can loosen the ink.
distractor_rationales.D: The ink releases acid and etches the paper.
distractor_rationales.B: Holes appear where the ink was thickest.

questions.stimulus: Tree rings are wide in years with abundant moisture and narrow in dry years. A stand of oaks on a dry ridge shows narrow rings in the same years as a stand in a wet valley nearby. Because both stands respond to the same regional rainfall, the shared pattern lets researchers cross-date the two records and build one longer chronology.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The two stands grew at different rates and cannot be compared.
Wide rings indicate drought at both sites.
A climate signal common to both sites allows their rings to be aligned in time.
Cross-dating depends on counting rings from the outside inward.

questions.explanation: A shared rainfall signal produces matching narrow years that align the chronologies.

distractor_rationales.A: The shared narrow years make alignment possible.
distractor_rationales.B: Wide rings indicate moisture, not drought.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage explains alignment by shared climate, not by a counting direction.

questions.stimulus: A foraging bee that finds a rich patch returns to the hive and performs a figure-eight dance. The angle of the dance's straight run relative to vertical corresponds to the direction of the food relative to the sun. When researchers rotated the hive, the dancers adjusted the angle, and the other bees still found the patch.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The dance encodes direction in a way that stays accurate as the hive's orientation changes.
Rotating the hive made the other bees unable to find the patch.
The dance communicates only the distance to food, not its direction.
The angle of the dance is fixed and unrelated to the sun.

questions.explanation: Adjustment after rotation shows the angle carries usable directional information.

distractor_rationales.C: The angle corresponds to direction.
distractor_rationales.B: The bees still found the patch after rotation.
distractor_rationales.D: The angle is measured relative to the sun.

questions.stimulus: Roman fish sauce was made by packing fish with salt and leaving the mixture in the sun for weeks. The salt drew water out of the tissue and suppressed the bacteria that would otherwise spoil it. Amphorae found on shipwrecks still contain residues of the sauce, and their sealed interiors kept the contents from exchanging with seawater.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The sauce survived because seawater flushed through the amphorae.
Salt encouraged the bacteria that spoil fish.
The residues found on shipwrecks are unrelated to fish sauce.
Salt preservation and sealed storage together kept the sauce chemically distinct for centuries.

questions.explanation: Preservation plus sealing explains why residues survived intact.

distractor_rationales.A: Sealed interiors are said to have kept seawater out.
distractor_rationales.B: Salt suppressed spoilage bacteria.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage identifies the residues as the sauce.

questions.stimulus: Deep-sea corals grow in cold water and lack the algae that feed shallow reefs. They capture food from passing currents instead, and their skeletons grow slowly enough that a colony may be centuries old. Radiocarbon dating of a specimen showed that its base was far older than its living branches, so the colony is best understood as a long-lived structure rather than a single animal.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Deep-sea corals depend on algae for food.
The living branches are the oldest part of the colony.
The age of a coral colony is set by the whole structure, not only by its living tissue.
Cold-water corals grow faster than shallow-water corals.

questions.explanation: Dating the base older than the branches shows the structure's age spans the whole colony.

distractor_rationales.D: The passage says their skeletons grow slowly.
distractor_rationales.B: The base is older than the living branches.
distractor_rationales.A: They lack symbiotic algae and catch food from currents.

questions.stimulus: Readers of old books sometimes wrote in the margins. A note may correct a printer's error, argue with the author, or record the date a reader finished the volume. Because marginalia are attached to a specific copy, they can show how one book traveled between owners. Historians therefore treat them as evidence of reading practice rather than as damage to be removed.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: All marginal notes record the same kind of information.
The value of marginalia lies in what they reveal about the people who used a particular copy.
Removing marginalia improves the historical record.
Marginalia are valuable mainly because they restore the printed text.

questions.explanation: The notes attach evidence of reading and ownership to a specific copy.

distractor_rationales.D: Their value is evidence of use, not restoration.
distractor_rationales.A: The passage lists several different kinds of note.
distractor_rationales.C: Historians treat the notes as evidence, not damage.

questions.stimulus: A retreating glacier leaves a valley with steep sides and a flat floor. A river valley of similar size usually has a V-shaped cross-section, because running water cuts downward and inward. The U-shape of a glaciated valley therefore records that ice, which erodes sideways as well as downward, once filled the space.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The shape of a valley can indicate whether ice or a river formed it.
Valley shape is unrelated to the agent of erosion.
A retreating glacier leaves a deep V-shaped trench.
Rivers carve U-shaped valleys more often than glaciers do.

questions.explanation: The contrast between U- and V-shaped profiles is the evidence for the erosional agent.

distractor_rationales.D: The text attributes U-shapes to ice and V-shapes to rivers.
distractor_rationales.C: Glacial valleys are described as U-shaped.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage draws the conclusion from shape.

questions.stimulus: Coffee grown under shade trees ripens more slowly than coffee grown in full sun. The slower ripening produces denser beans, and tasters often describe the cup as more complex. Yields per hectare, however, are lower under shade, and farmers must weigh the price premium against the reduced volume harvested.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Shade-grown coffee can earn more per bean while producing fewer beans overall.
Shade trees raise yields without affecting quality.
Shade-grown coffee always earns more per hectare than sun-grown coffee.
Full-sun coffee produces denser beans than shade-grown coffee.

questions.explanation: Quality and price rise while volume falls, creating a trade-off.

distractor_rationales.C: The passage says yields are lower, so per-hectare earnings are not guaranteed.
distractor_rationales.D: Slower ripening under shade produces denser beans.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says shade lowers yields.

questions.stimulus: Honey often contains pollen grains from the flowers the bees visited. Because pollen grains have distinctive shapes, a sample can reveal which plants were in bloom. Analysis of a jar from a market stall showed pollen from a plant that flowers only in early spring, several months before the honey was sold. The jar was probably not from the most recent harvest.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Pollen analysis cannot distinguish one season's honey from another's.
Bees visit only one plant species in a season.
The jar was certainly made from artificial honey.
Pollen can date honey by showing which flowering season produced it.

questions.explanation: Season-specific pollen in a jar sold later points to an earlier harvest.

distractor_rationales.A: Distinctive pollen tied to a season is exactly what enables dating.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage infers age, not adulteration.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage describes pollen from visited flowers generally.

questions.stimulus: Shipworms bore into wooden hulls and pilings, digesting the wood with the help of bacteria. A hull recovered from a cold, low-oxygen harbour showed far less damage than one from a warm estuary. Conservators now store excavated timbers in tanks where oxygen is limited, because the animals that attack wood need oxygen as well as wood.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Warm water protects wood from shipworms.
Oxygen has no effect on wood-boring animals.
Limiting oxygen slows the organisms that would otherwise consume waterlogged wood.
Shipworms digest wood without the help of bacteria.

questions.explanation: The comparison and the storage practice both turn on oxygen.

distractor_rationales.A: The warm estuary showed more damage.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage mentions bacterial help.
distractor_rationales.B: The storage method relies on oxygen limitation.

questions.stimulus: A solar still collects drinking water by evaporating brine under a transparent cover and condensing the vapour on the underside. Output depends on sunlight and on the area of the cover. On a cloudy day a small still may produce only a few spoonfuls, while a larger still in full sun produces liters. The device is therefore a supplement rather than a stand-alone supply.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Condensation reduces the amount of water collected.
A solar still's output is too weather-dependent to guarantee water on its own.
A solar still produces the same output in all weather.
Small stills outperform large ones in full sun.

questions.explanation: Variable output under clouds explains why the device is a supplement.

distractor_rationales.C: The passage describes output varying with sunlight and area.
distractor_rationales.D: Larger stills in full sun produce liters.
distractor_rationales.A: Condensation is the collection step.

questions.stimulus: Fish ferment faster in warm weather, and salt slows the process. Communities that live where temperatures stay high use more salt in their preserved fish than communities in cooler regions. A recipe that works in one place can therefore fail in another, not because the method is wrong but because the conditions have changed.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Preservation recipes have to be adjusted to local temperature.
Salt speeds fermentation in warm weather.
Cooler regions require more salt than warmer ones.
A recipe that works in one region always works in another.

questions.explanation: Temperature changes the rate of fermentation, so salt amounts must adapt.

distractor_rationales.B: Salt slows fermentation.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says warmer communities use more salt.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage says a recipe can fail when conditions change.

questions.stimulus: A cathedral bell is tuned by grinding metal from its rim. Removing material lowers the pitch and can also change the relationships among the bell's partial tones. Founders therefore remove metal in small stages, testing between each. A bell ground too far cannot be restored, because the metal cannot be added back.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Tuning is irreversible, so it proceeds cautiously and in measured steps.
Grinding raises the pitch of a bell.
Partial tones are unaffected by removing metal.
Founders grind the rim quickly because extra metal can be added later.

questions.explanation: Irreversibility explains the incremental method.

distractor_rationales.D: Metal cannot be added back.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage says removing material lowers pitch.
distractor_rationales.C: Grinding can change the partial relationships.

questions.stimulus: Compacted soil resists root growth even when it holds enough water. Roots follow pores and cracks, and compaction closes those channels. In a field where machinery has passed repeatedly, roots may spread sideways above a hard layer instead of reaching deeper moisture. The plants survive but depend on rain in the upper soil.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Compaction makes crops more vulnerable to drought in the upper soil.
Roots grow through compacted soil more easily than through pores.
Machinery traffic improves the soil's pore structure.
Compaction helps roots reach deeper water.

questions.explanation: Shallow rooting ties survival to upper-soil moisture.

distractor_rationales.D: Roots are blocked from deeper layers.
distractor_rationales.B: Roots follow pores, which compaction closes.
distractor_rationales.C: Traffic is the cause of the compaction described.

questions.stimulus: Soot deposits on cave ceilings accumulate in thin layers that record the fires below. A layer rich in charcoal indicates a larger or more frequent fire; a gap indicates a period without burning. Archaeologists reading a sequence of layers can therefore reconstruct how often people used a cave, even when no tools survive.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Soot layers form only when a cave is empty of people.
Soot layers provide a record of human activity independent of artefacts.
Charcoal-rich layers indicate cold weather rather than fires.
A gap in the layers proves that the cave was never visited.

questions.explanation: Burning evidence alone can show occupation frequency.

distractor_rationales.A: The passage says the layers record use.
distractor_rationales.D: A gap indicates a period without burning, not no visits.
distractor_rationales.C: Charcoal richness tracks fire size or frequency.

questions.stimulus: Harbour sediment traps lead, copper and organic matter washed from streets and ships. A core taken near a former shipyard contains a sharp peak in copper at the depth corresponding to the yard's busiest decades. Above that layer, concentrations fall as the yard closed and runoff was diverted. The core therefore reads as a history of industrial activity.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Chemical layers in harbour mud can be tied to the rise and fall of nearby industry.
Copper concentrations rise after the shipyard closed.
Harbour sediment carries no trace of industrial activity.
The peak in copper came from natural erosion only.

questions.explanation: The copper profile matches the yard's timeline.

distractor_rationales.B: Concentrations fall above the peak as the yard closed.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage describes clear traces.
distractor_rationales.D: The peak corresponds to the yard's busiest decades.

questions.stimulus: Bats that hibernate through winter need high humidity as well as steady cold. Dry air draws water from their skin and wings, and an aroused bat burns fat it cannot replace until spring. A cave that is cold but draughty can therefore be worse for a colony than one that is slightly warmer but still.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Bats can replace fat easily during winter.
Air movement has no effect on hibernating bats.
Stable, humid conditions matter more to hibernating bats than cold alone.
Warm, dry caves are ideal for hibernating bats.

questions.explanation: Humidity and stillness protect the fat reserve that must last the winter.

distractor_rationales.D: Dry air causes water loss and arousal.
distractor_rationales.A: The passage says fat cannot be replaced until spring.
distractor_rationales.B: Draughty caves are described as harmful.

questions.stimulus: Roof tiles are laid so that each row overlaps the one below. Water running down the slope crosses from one tile to the next without reaching the deck beneath. If the overlap is too small, wind-driven rain can be forced upward under the edge. The overlap is therefore a specification, not a decorative choice.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Overlap width must be set to withstand the weather a roof will face.
The overlap has no effect on whether rain reaches the deck.
Water runs upward across the roof under normal conditions.
A smaller overlap gives better protection in strong wind.

questions.explanation: Weather exposure sets the minimum overlap.

distractor_rationales.D: Too small an overlap lets wind-driven rain under the edge.
distractor_rationales.C: Water runs down the slope; only driven rain moves upward.
distractor_rationales.B: The overlap determines whether water crosses safely.

questions.stimulus: Some plants rely on ants to carry their seeds. The seed carries a fleshy appendage that ants eat, and the seed itself is discarded underground. Seeds moved this way end up buried, where they escape drying and some seed-eaters. The plant pays a small food cost for dispersal and burial.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Seeds left on the surface survive better than buried ones.
The food reward buys the seed both transport and a safer place to germinate.
Ants destroy the seeds they carry.
The appendage prevents ants from moving the seed.

questions.explanation: Transport plus burial explains the benefit of the food cost.

distractor_rationales.C: The seed is discarded intact underground.
distractor_rationales.D: The appendage is the reward that attracts ants.
distractor_rationales.A: Burial is described as protection.

questions.stimulus: Clipper ships carried tea from China to London, and speed mattered because early arrivals sold at higher prices. Their hulls were narrow and their sail area large, which made them fast in strong winds but hard to handle in a calm. After steamships offered reliable schedules, the clippers lost their advantage.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Reliability of arrival proved more valuable than the fastest possible passage.
Clippers remained the fastest option after steamships appeared.
Speed had no effect on the price tea fetched.
Calm weather was the clippers' greatest advantage.

questions.explanation: Steam's dependable schedule displaced the clipper's speed premium.

distractor_rationales.B: Clippers lost their advantage to steamships.
distractor_rationales.D: The narrow hull was hard to handle in a calm.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says early arrivals sold higher.

questions.stimulus: Some birds lay eggs with thinner shells where the soil is low in calcium. The birds cannot manufacture calcium, so they must take it from food or grit. Studies of a population on calcium-poor ground found thinner shells and more breakages than in a population on limestone. The difference tracked geology, not species.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Birds can synthesise calcium without eating it.
Access to calcium in the environment shapes shell thickness in these birds.
Shell thickness is fixed by the species and cannot vary.

questions.explanation: The geologic contrast, with the same species, isolates calcium availability.

distractor_rationales.D: The two populations differ within the same species.
distractor_rationales.B: Thin shells occur on poor ground.
distractor_rationales.A: The passage says birds must obtain calcium from food or grit.

questions.stimulus: Residue inside Roman amphorae can be identified by its chemical signature. Jars found in a storage room contained traces of olive oil, while jars from a nearby shop contained fish sauce. The two sets were the same shape. Shape alone therefore does not tell an archaeologist what a vessel carried.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Fish sauce and olive oil leave identical residues.
Contents must be identified chemically, because form does not reveal use.
All jars in a storage room held the same product.
Amphora shape reliably indicates what was stored inside.

questions.explanation: Same shape, different contents forces chemical identification.

distractor_rationales.D: Identical shapes held different contents.
distractor_rationales.A: The distinction comes from chemical signatures.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage contrasts two nearby sets.

questions.stimulus: Pencil leads are graded by hardness, which depends on the ratio of graphite to clay. More clay makes a harder lead that holds a sharp point and prints lightly; more graphite makes a softer lead that darkens the page and wears quickly. A drafter choosing a lead is choosing between precision and darkness.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: The graphite-to-clay ratio has no effect on wear.
Hard leads darken the page more than soft leads.
No single lead suits both fine detail and dense shading equally well.
Clay increases the darkness of a pencil line.

questions.explanation: The trade-off between point retention and darkness is the basis of the grading scale.

distractor_rationales.B: Hard leads print lightly; soft leads darken.
distractor_rationales.D: Graphite provides darkness, not clay.
distractor_rationales.A: The ratio determines both darkness and wear.

questions.stimulus: A bleached coral reef can recover if the algae that live inside the coral return while the coral is still alive. Recovery is slower where the reef is also stressed by sediment or warm water. Surveys find that reefs with cleaner water regain color sooner after a bleaching event than reefs near river mouths.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Bleached coral is always dead and cannot recover.
Sediment speeds the return of algae to coral.
Warm water improves recovery after bleaching.
Reducing local stress helps a reef recover from bleaching.

questions.explanation: The comparison points to local stress as a brake on recovery.

distractor_rationales.B: Cleaner-water reefs recovered sooner.
distractor_rationales.A: The passage describes recovery while the coral is alive.
distractor_rationales.C: Warm water is named as an additional stress.

questions.stimulus: Salmon that die after spawning leave carcasses in streams. Their bodies carry nitrogen from the ocean, which enters the food web as the carcasses decay. Trees along a stream with many spawning salmon contain more marine-derived nitrogen than trees along a stream without them. The forest is therefore linked to the ocean by the fish.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Marine nutrients reach streamside forests through the bodies of spawning fish.
Trees cannot take up nitrogen from decaying fish.
Salmon remove nitrogen from streamside forests.
The connection exists only in streams without spawning salmon.

questions.explanation: The nitrogen signature in trees traces the marine source through the carcasses.

distractor_rationales.B: The passage reports elevated nitrogen in those trees.
distractor_rationales.C: The carcasses add nitrogen.
distractor_rationales.D: The contrast is between streams with and without salmon.

questions.stimulus: A windmill's sails turn a shaft, and gearing converts that slow, powerful rotation into a faster one at the millstone. Changing the gear ratio changes the speed of the stone without changing the wind. Millers keep several gears on hand so that a strong wind and a light one can both be used.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Gearing lets a miller match the stone's speed to the available wind.
A single fixed gear ratio suits every wind condition.
The millstone turns more slowly than the shaft in all gears.
Gearing changes the amount of wind reaching the sails.

questions.explanation: Multiple gears exist to keep stone speed steady across wind strengths.

distractor_rationales.D: Gearing converts rotation, not wind.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage describes changing ratios for different winds.
distractor_rationales.C: The gearing speeds the rotation up at the stone.

questions.stimulus: A manuscript written with acidic ink can lose text at the same time it loses paper. Washing a leaf removes acid but may also lift the ink, so conservators first test a small, unimportant area. If the ink survives the test, the leaf can be washed; if not, it is stored dry and digitised instead.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Every leaf can be washed safely with acidic ink.
Testing a small area damages the whole manuscript.
Digitisation removes acid from the paper.
Treatment decisions depend on evidence from a test before the whole leaf is exposed.

questions.explanation: The small-area test governs whether the full treatment is safe.

distractor_rationales.A: Washing may lift the ink.
distractor_rationales.B: The test uses an unimportant area precisely to avoid damage.
distractor_rationales.C: Digitisation creates a copy; it does not treat the paper.

questions.stimulus: Moss on a stone wall is thickest on the side that receives the most moisture, not always the side that receives the most light. On a wall shaded by trees, moss may cover the whole face, while an exposed wall carries moss in a band near the ground. Anyone reading moss as a compass would need to know the local conditions.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Moss requires full sunlight and avoids damp surfaces.
Moss always grows on the north side of a wall regardless of shade.
A shaded wall carries less moss than an exposed one.
Moss growth reflects moisture and shade, so it is an unreliable direction indicator without local context.

questions.explanation: Moisture and shade dominate, which defeats naive compass use.

distractor_rationales.B: The passage says moisture matters more than direction.
distractor_rationales.A: Moss is thickest where moisture is greatest.
distractor_rationales.C: The shaded wall may be covered entirely.

questions.stimulus: Volcanic lightning occurs in ash clouds when particles collide and separate charge. The effect is more common in eruptions that produce fine ash and vigorous convection. Observers have used lightning detection to track eruptions at night and in bad weather, when cameras see little. The electrical signal becomes a remote sensing tool.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Volcanic lightning occurs only in eruptions with no ash.
Cameras see eruptions better at night than detectors do.
Lightning detection replaces the need to monitor volcanoes.
Detecting lightning can reveal an eruption that visibility would hide.

questions.explanation: The electrical signal works when visual observation fails.

distractor_rationales.A: The passage ties lightning to fine ash and convection.
distractor_rationales.C: It is a tool, not a replacement for monitoring.
distractor_rationales.B: The text says cameras see little at night and in bad weather.

questions.stimulus: Wool takes dye unevenly if its scales are damaged. Makers therefore clean fleece gently and avoid sudden temperature changes during dyeing, since a rapid shift can shock the fibres. A dye lot that looks patchy often records a handling error rather than a fault in the dye itself.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Rapid temperature changes improve the evenness of dye uptake.
Damaged scales help wool absorb dye uniformly.
Even color depends on gentle handling as much as on the dye recipe.
Patchiness always indicates a faulty dye.

questions.explanation: Handling errors, not the dye, explain many patchy lots.

distractor_rationales.A: The passage warns that rapid shifts shock the fibres.
distractor_rationales.B: Damage is described as causing uneven uptake.
distractor_rationales.D: Patchiness often reflects handling, not the dye.

questions.stimulus: Charcoal in lake sediment comes from fires in the surrounding catchment. A layer with abundant charcoal often coincides with a shift from forest pollen to grass pollen. The two signals together suggest that fire removed trees and allowed grasses to spread. Neither signal alone would establish the sequence.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: Charcoal layers indicate that no fire occurred in the catchment.
Combining charcoal and pollen evidence links fire to vegetation change.
Pollen shifts always precede fires by several centuries.
Grass pollen excludes the possibility of fire.

questions.explanation: The coincidence of the two proxies is what ties fire to the vegetation shift.

distractor_rationales.A: Charcoal records fire.
distractor_rationales.C: The signals are described as coinciding.
distractor_rationales.D: Grass pollen follows fire in the proposed sequence.

questions.stimulus: A tea clipper's narrow hull reduced drag but also reduced cargo space. Owners packed light, high-value cargo such as tea and raced for the first market. When the Suez Canal opened, steamships could take a shorter route that sailing ships could not use reliably. The clippers' advantage narrowed.
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: A route change reduced the value of the clippers' speed and small capacity.
